Asparagus.about: British asparagus has a short season that traditionally runs from late April to midsummer, ending around the summer solstice. The spears are sweet, grassy and nutty, and they lose sweetness fast once cut, so home-grown spears picked that week beat imported ones easily. The Vale of Evesham in Worcestershire is the best-known growing area.
Asparagus.choose: Look for firm, straight spears with tight, closed tips and moist ends that haven't dried out or gone woody.
Asparagus.store: Stand the spears upright in a glass of water in the fridge, loosely covered, and eat within two or three days.
Asparagus.prep: Snap off the woody base where it naturally breaks, then steam, boil for three or four minutes, or char on a griddle. Serve with melted butter, hollandaise or a soft-boiled egg for dipping.
Asparagus.waste: Snap off the woody ends and simmer them with onion and herb stalks for a stock, then use it as the base for asparagus soup or risotto.

Globe artichokes.about: Globe artichokes are the flower buds of a large thistle, with a sweet, nutty flavour and a faintly bitter edge. British-grown heads appear from early summer into autumn, and smaller ones can be cooked whole. Eating them leaf by leaf, dipped in butter or vinaigrette, is a slow summer pleasure.
Globe artichokes.choose: Choose heavy heads with tightly closed, squeaky leaves and a fresh green colour, avoiding any that are dry, splayed or browning at the tips.
Globe artichokes.store: Keep in a plastic bag in the fridge and cook within three or four days.
Globe artichokes.prep: Rub cut surfaces with lemon to stop browning, then boil or steam whole until a leaf pulls away easily, or trim down to the heart and remove the hairy choke. Hearts are good braised with wine and herbs or roasted.
Globe artichokes.waste: Peel the tough outer layer from the stems and cook the tender core with the hearts, and simmer the trimmed leaves in water for a light stock.

Aubergines.about: Aubergines have a mild, slightly bitter flesh that turns soft and creamy when cooked properly and soaks up oil and spices well. British crops are glasshouse-grown, mostly in late summer, and are often firmer and fresher than imports. Look out for smaller varieties and striped or pale violet types at markets.
Aubergines.choose: Pick firm, heavy aubergines with tight, glossy skin and a fresh green stalk, avoiding soft patches or wrinkles.
Aubergines.store: Store in a cool place or the salad drawer of the fridge and use within four or five days.
Aubergines.prep: Cook until fully soft: roast in chunks, slice and grill, or char whole over a flame for a smoky dip. They suit curries, moussaka, caponata and miso glazes.
Aubergines.waste: Use the soft trimmings and any slightly wrinkled aubergines in baba ganoush or caponata, where long cooking or charring hides any loss of texture.

Beetroot.about: Beetroot is an earthy, sweet root that comes in deep red, golden and pink-and-white striped Chioggia varieties. British beetroot runs from early summer, when young bunches come with usable leaves, through to winter from store. Roasting concentrates its sugars, while raw grated beetroot is crisp and fresh.
Beetroot.choose: Choose firm, smooth roots that feel heavy, and if the leaves are attached they should be perky and unwilted.
Beetroot.store: Twist off the leaves (cook them like chard) and keep roots in the fridge for up to two weeks.
Beetroot.prep: Roast whole in foil or boil in the skin, then rub off the skin once cool; small roots can be grated raw into salads. Wear gloves or prep on a plate to avoid staining.
Beetroot.waste: Cook the young leaves and stems like chard, and grate any odd ends of root into slaw, or roast and blitz them into a dip.

Broad beans.about: Broad beans are one of the first British summer pulses, sweet and slightly grassy when young. Early pods hold small, tender beans that can be eaten raw; later in the season they grow larger and starchier and benefit from double podding. Young tops of the plant are also edible, cooked like spinach.
Broad beans.choose: Look for firm, bright green pods that feel full but not bulging, and avoid any that are blackened or limp.
Broad beans.store: Keep pods in the fridge and use within two or three days, as the beans turn starchy over time.
Broad beans.prep: Pod, blanch for a minute or two, then slip larger beans out of their grey skins. Toss with herbs and olive oil, mash onto toast, or add to risotto and salads.
Broad beans.waste: Very young pods can be sliced and cooked whole, and a quick blanch makes the tough grey skins easy to slip off older beans for a brighter purée.

Broccoli (calabrese).about: Calabrese is the familiar green-headed broccoli, sweet and mildly grassy with a tender stalk. It is imported much of the year, but British heads cut through summer and early autumn are fresher and sweeter. The stalk is good eating too, peeled and sliced.
Broccoli (calabrese).choose: Choose tight, dark green heads with no yellowing florets and a firm, freshly cut stalk.
Broccoli (calabrese).store: Keep unwashed in the fridge in a loosely closed bag and use within four or five days.
Broccoli (calabrese).prep: Cut into florets and peel and slice the stalk, then steam, stir-fry or roast at high heat until the edges char. Avoid overcooking, which brings out sulphurous flavours.
Broccoli (calabrese).waste: Peel the thick stalk, then slice it into stir-fries or grate it into slaw, and cook the leaves like any other greens.

Purple sprouting broccoli.about: Purple sprouting broccoli is a British late-winter and spring favourite, cropping in the hungry gap when little else is growing. The slim stems and purple florets are sweeter and more intense than calabrese, with a slight bitterness. The purple colour turns green as it cooks.
Purple sprouting broccoli.choose: Look for crisp stems that snap cleanly, tight purple heads and fresh leaves, with no yellowing or slimy patches.
Purple sprouting broccoli.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and eat within three days.
Purple sprouting broccoli.prep: Trim the woody ends and peel thick stems, then steam, boil briefly or roast. It is classic with hollandaise or anchovy butter, or tossed through pasta with chilli and garlic.
Purple sprouting broccoli.waste: The leaves and thicker stems are just as good as the florets, so slice the stems thinly and cook everything together.

Brussels sprouts.about: Brussels sprouts are small, tightly packed buds that grow up a tall stalk, with a nutty, mildly bitter flavour that sweetens after a frost. They peak around Christmas, and much of the UK crop comes from Lincolnshire. Treated well, they are very different from the overboiled sprouts of school dinners.
Brussels sprouts.choose: Choose small to medium, firm, tightly closed sprouts with bright green leaves, or buy them on the stalk, where they keep better.
Brussels sprouts.store: Keep in the fridge and use within a week; on the stalk they last a little longer in a cool place.
Brussels sprouts.prep: Trim the base and peel off any tired outer leaves, then roast halves until caramelised, shred raw into salads or stir-fry. If boiling, cook briefly and drain well.
Brussels sprouts.waste: Shred the loose outer leaves and fry them until crisp, and use up leftover cooked sprouts in bubble and squeak.

Brussels tops.about: Brussels tops are the leafy crown at the head of the sprout stalk, picked once the sprouts have been harvested. They taste like a mild, sweet cabbage with a sprout-like nuttiness. They are often cheap at farmers' markets and greengrocers in winter, and they make a good alternative to spring greens.
Brussels tops.choose: Look for bright, crisp leaves with no yellowing or slimy patches at the base.
Brussels tops.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three or four days.
Brussels tops.prep: Shred and remove any thick ribs, then steam, stir-fry with garlic, or wilt in butter. They are good in bubble and squeak.
Brussels tops.waste: Cook the whole leafy head like spring greens, and slice the firmer central stems thinly so they cook at the same rate as the leaves.

Butternut squash.about: Butternut squash is a bell-shaped winter squash with dense, sweet orange flesh and a nutty flavour. British squash is harvested in autumn and cured so it keeps for months. It is reliable and easy to peel, and it works in soups, roasts and risottos.
Butternut squash.choose: Choose a squash that feels heavy for its size, with matt, unblemished skin and a firm, dry stalk.
Butternut squash.store: Keep whole in a cool, dry place for two to three months; once cut, wrap and refrigerate for up to five days.
Butternut squash.prep: Peel with a sturdy peeler, scoop out the seeds and roast in wedges or chunks until caramelised. It also makes smooth soups, and the roasted seeds are a good snack.
Butternut squash.waste: Wash the seeds, toss them in oil and salt and roast them as a snack, and leave the skin on when roasting chunks as it softens and is edible.

Crown Prince squash.about: Crown Prince is a blue-grey skinned winter squash with dense, deep orange flesh. It is sweeter and drier than butternut, with a nutty flavour, and many cooks rate it the best squash for eating. It stores very well, so British-grown ones last well into the new year.
Crown Prince squash.choose: Choose one with hard, unblemished skin, a dry, corky stalk and a good weight for its size.
Crown Prince squash.store: Store whole somewhere cool and dry for up to three or four months; wrap cut pieces and refrigerate for up to five days.
Crown Prince squash.prep: The skin is very hard, so cut carefully with a heavy knife, then roast in wedges with the skin on, or peel and simmer for soup. It roasts beautifully with little more than oil and salt.
Crown Prince squash.waste: Roast the seeds as a crunchy snack or soup topping, and simmer peelings and fibrous bits from the centre with onion for a sweet stock.

Pumpkin.about: Most pumpkins sold in Britain around Halloween are carving types with watery, bland flesh. Culinary varieties such as Queensland Blue, Musquée de Provence or small Sugar Pie pumpkins have sweeter, denser flesh that is worth cooking. Their season runs through autumn.
Pumpkin.choose: Ask for an eating variety if you plan to cook it, and choose one that feels heavy with firm skin and an intact, dry stalk.
Pumpkin.store: Keep whole in a cool, dry place for a month or more; refrigerate cut pieces wrapped and use within five days.
Pumpkin.prep: Peel, deseed and roast in chunks, or simmer for soups and purées. Purée is good in pies and bread, and the seeds can be roasted with salt.
Pumpkin.waste: Roast the seeds with oil and salt, and use any leftover carved or cooked flesh in soup, curry or a spiced loaf rather than throwing it away.

Savoy cabbage.about: Savoy cabbage has deeply crinkled, dark green outer leaves and a sweet, mild flavour. It is one of the hardiest British winter cabbages and holds its texture well when cooked. The crinkled leaves are good at catching butter and sauce.
Savoy cabbage.choose: Choose a heavy cabbage with crisp, deeply coloured outer leaves and no yellowing or holes.
Savoy cabbage.store: Keep whole in the fridge for up to two weeks, and wrap cut halves tightly.
Savoy cabbage.prep: Shred and steam or stir-fry briefly, or blanch whole leaves for stuffing. It is classic with bacon and onion, in bubble and squeak, or braised with cream.
Savoy cabbage.waste: Slice the core and the thick ribs thinly and add them to stir-fries or soups, and use the dark outer leaves for wrapping stuffings.

Red cabbage.about: Red cabbage is a dense, peppery cabbage that turns sweet and soft when slowly braised. It is a winter staple and stores well, so British heads last through to spring. Braised red cabbage with apple and spices is a traditional part of Christmas dinner in many homes.
Red cabbage.choose: Choose firm, heavy heads with glossy, tightly packed leaves.
Red cabbage.store: Keep whole in the fridge for two weeks or more; wrap cut halves and use within a week.
Red cabbage.prep: Shred finely and braise slowly with apple, vinegar and a little sugar, or slice raw into slaw. A splash of vinegar keeps the colour bright purple.
Red cabbage.waste: Finely shred the core with the leaves for slaw, and quick-pickle any leftover wedges in vinegar, sugar and salt to keep them for a week or two.

January King cabbage.about: January King is a hardy winter cabbage with blue-green leaves tinged with purple. It has a firm head and a sweet, nutty flavour, and it gets sweeter after frost. It is a traditional English variety that stands in the field through the coldest months.
January King cabbage.choose: Choose a heavy, firm head with crisp leaves and good purple colouring.
January King cabbage.store: Keep in the fridge for up to two weeks, and wrap cut pieces tightly.
January King cabbage.prep: Shred and steam, stir-fry or braise in butter, or cut into wedges and roast. It suits bacon, game and winter stews.
January King cabbage.waste: Use the tough outer leaves in soups or stews and slice the core thinly into stir-fries rather than throwing them away.

Hispi (pointed) cabbage.about: Hispi is a pointed, cone-shaped cabbage with tender, sweet leaves. It is softer and less dense than round cabbages, so it cooks quickly. Charred or roasted hispi has become a popular restaurant dish, and British crops run from late spring into autumn.
Hispi (pointed) cabbage.choose: Choose a firm, tightly packed head with bright green, glossy leaves and no splits.
Hispi (pointed) cabbage.store: Keep in the fridge and use within a week.
Hispi (pointed) cabbage.prep: Cut into wedges and char in a hot pan or roast until the edges blacken and the centre is tender, or shred and stir-fry. It is also good raw in slaws.
Hispi (pointed) cabbage.waste: Char leftover wedges in a hot pan for a side dish, and slice the core finely into slaw or stir-fries.

Spring greens.about: Spring greens are young cabbages picked before a heart forms, with loose, dark green leaves. They are tender, sweet and slightly bitter, and they fill the gap in early spring when other greens are scarce. Cooked quickly, they keep their colour and a pleasant bite, and they are usually cheap and plentiful at greengrocers in March and April.
Spring greens.choose: Look for bright, crisp leaves with no yellowing, wilting or slimy stems.
Spring greens.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three days.
Spring greens.prep: Remove any tough central ribs, shred and wilt quickly in butter or olive oil with garlic. They suit stews, soups and Asian-style stir-fries.
Spring greens.waste: Slice the thick central stalks thinly and start cooking them a minute or two before the leaves so everything ends up tender.

Carrots.about: Carrots are a reliable staple, sweet and earthy, and British carrots are available for most of the year from field and store. Early bunched carrots in summer are especially sweet and tender. Coloured heritage types in purple, yellow and white are now common at markets.
Carrots.choose: Choose firm, smooth carrots with no cracks or soft spots, and if the tops are on they should be fresh and green.
Carrots.store: Remove leafy tops, then keep carrots in the fridge for two to three weeks.
Carrots.prep: Young carrots just need a scrub; older ones can be peeled. Roast with honey and cumin, glaze in butter, grate raw into salads or use as a base for stocks and stews.
Carrots.waste: Scrub rather than peel, blitz the feathery tops into a pesto or salsa verde with other herbs, and add any peelings to the stock bag.

Cauliflower.about: Cauliflower is grown in Britain all year, with Cornwall and Lincolnshire major growers, and it is at its best in winter and early spring. Its creamy white curd is mild and nutty, and it turns sweet when roasted. Purple, green and orange types are also available.
Cauliflower.choose: Choose a heavy head with tight, creamy-white curds and crisp, fresh green leaves wrapped around it.
Cauliflower.store: Keep in the fridge, loosely wrapped, and use within five days.
Cauliflower.prep: Cut into florets, or slice into steaks, then roast at high heat, steam, or bake in cheese sauce. The leaves can be roasted too.
Cauliflower.waste: Roast the outer leaves until crisp at the edges and slice the core thinly to cook with the florets, as both are sweet and tender.

Romanesco.about: Romanesco is a lime-green relative of cauliflower with pointed, spiralling florets that form a natural fractal pattern. Its flavour is nuttier and sweeter than cauliflower, and its texture is firmer, so it holds its shape well when cooked. British-grown heads are available in late summer and autumn, and they are freshest from farmers' markets.
Romanesco.choose: Choose heavy, bright green heads with firm points and no browning or soft spots.
Romanesco.store: Keep in the fridge and use within five days.
Romanesco.prep: Break into florets and steam briefly, roast, or toss into pasta. Keep the cooking short so it holds its shape and colour.
Romanesco.waste: Treat the leaves and core as you would cauliflower: roast the leaves and slice the core thinly to cook alongside the florets.

Celeriac.about: Celeriac is the knobbly swollen root of a type of celery, with a mild celery flavour and a nutty sweetness. It is a classic British winter vegetable that stores well. It is excellent raw in remoulade, and it makes a smooth mash or soup.
Celeriac.choose: Choose firm, heavy roots that are not hollow-sounding, and avoid soft patches or excessive knobbles that make peeling wasteful.
Celeriac.store: Keep in the fridge for two to three weeks; once cut, wrap tightly and drop pieces in lemony water to stop them browning.
Celeriac.prep: Cut away the skin with a knife, then grate raw for remoulade, roast in chunks, mash with potatoes or roast whole. It pairs well with game and rich meats.
Celeriac.waste: Scrub the knobbly peel well and simmer it in stock, and use any leftover root in mash, soup or a grated remoulade.

Celery.about: Celery is crisp, juicy and savoury, with a slight bitterness. Fen celery, grown in the black soils of Cambridgeshire and earthed up to keep it pale, has Protected Geographical Indication status and is harvested in autumn. It is also the base of many stocks and soups.
Celery.choose: Choose tight, crisp heads with firm, unbendable stalks and fresh leaves.
Celery.store: Wrap in a damp cloth or foil and keep in the fridge for up to two weeks.
Celery.prep: Wash between the stalks, then use raw with cheese, slice into salads, or braise whole hearts. The leaves are useful as a herb.
Celery.waste: Chop the leaves into salads, soups or salsa verde like a herb, and keep the bases and limp sticks in the freezer for stock.

Swiss chard.about: Swiss chard has broad, glossy leaves and thick white stalks with a mild, earthy flavour similar to spinach. It grows easily in Britain and crops from summer into late autumn. The leaves and stalks are best cooked separately because the stalks take longer.
Swiss chard.choose: Look for crisp, glossy leaves and firm stalks with no limp or yellowing patches.
Swiss chard.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three or four days.
Swiss chard.prep: Separate the stalks and leaves; cook chopped stalks first, then add leaves to wilt. Stalks can also be gratinéed with cream and cheese.
Swiss chard.waste: Slice the stems and cook them a few minutes before adding the leaves, or pickle them, rather than discarding them.

Rainbow chard.about: Rainbow chard is a mix of chard varieties with stalks in red, yellow, orange and pink. The flavour is earthy and mineral, like spinach with more body. It crops from summer to autumn in British gardens and is widely available at markets.
Rainbow chard.choose: Choose crisp, bright stalks and glossy, unblemished leaves.
Rainbow chard.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three or four days.
Rainbow chard.prep: Separate the stalks and leaves, cook the chopped stalks first and add the leaves at the end. It is good sautéed with garlic, in gratins, or folded into frittatas.
Rainbow chard.waste: Cook the colourful stems first, then add the leaves, or quick-pickle the stems in vinegar for a bright relish.

Chicory.about: Chicory, also called endive, is grown in the dark to produce tight, pale heads with a crisp texture and gentle bitterness. White and red forms are available, and it is at its best in winter. It works raw in salads or braised until soft and sweet.
Chicory.choose: Choose tight, firm heads with pale yellow tips; green tips mean they have been exposed to light and will be more bitter.
Chicory.store: Wrap in paper and keep in the fridge, away from light, for up to a week.
Chicory.prep: Remove the outer leaves and use the rest raw in salads, or halve and braise in butter until golden. It suits blue cheese, orange and walnuts.
Chicory.waste: Bitter outer leaves are good braised with butter and a little orange juice, and leftover heads can be halved and griddled.

Radicchio.about: Radicchio is a red-leafed chicory with a pronounced bitter flavour and crisp texture. Types include the round Chioggia and the long-leaved Treviso, and some are now grown in Britain. It is at its best through the colder months, when its bitterness is balanced by sweeter winter ingredients.
Radicchio.choose: Look for firm, crisp heads with bright colour and no browning at the edges.
Radicchio.store: Keep wrapped in the fridge for up to a week.
Radicchio.prep: Use raw in salads, or quarter and grill or roast to soften the bitterness. It is good in risotto and with sweet fruit.
Radicchio.waste: Use the tougher outer leaves in a risotto or braise, where cooking softens their bitterness, and keep the crisp inner leaves for salads.

Courgettes.about: Courgettes are summer squash with a mild, sweet flavour and tender skin. British courgettes crop prolifically in July and August, and small, firm ones taste best. Round, yellow and pale green varieties are often found at farmers' markets.
Courgettes.choose: Choose small to medium courgettes that are firm, glossy and heavy for their size.
Courgettes.store: Keep in the fridge and use within four or five days.
Courgettes.prep: Slice and fry, griddle or roast, or grate raw into salads. Salting larger courgettes before cooking draws out water.
Courgettes.waste: Grate large or soft courgettes into fritters, cakes or pasta sauces, or freeze grated courgette in portions for winter soups.

Courgette flowers.about: Courgette flowers are the blossoms of the courgette plant, harvested in early summer. They have a delicate, slightly sweet flavour. They are fragile and seldom found in supermarkets, so they are a seasonal treat from markets or the garden.
Courgette flowers.choose: Choose bright, freshly picked flowers that are just open, with no wilting or browning.
Courgette flowers.store: Use on the day of picking if possible, or keep in the fridge laid on damp paper for a day at most.
Courgette flowers.prep: Remove the stamen or pistil and check for insects, then stuff with ricotta and herbs, and deep-fry in light batter or bake. They can also be torn raw into salads.
Courgette flowers.waste: If you are not stuffing them, tear any spare or slightly wilted flowers into pasta, risotto or an omelette at the last minute.

Cucumber.about: Cucumbers are cool, crisp and watery, with a fresh, mild flavour. British cucumbers are grown under glass, mostly in the Lea Valley and Yorkshire, and summer crops are the freshest. Shorter ridge and mini cucumbers have more flavour and crunch.
Cucumber.choose: Choose firm, dark green cucumbers that feel heavy and have no soft or yellowing patches.
Cucumber.store: Keep in the fridge and use within a week; wrap cut ends in cling film.
Cucumber.prep: Slice into salads and sandwiches, make quick pickles, or use in raita and tzatziki. Salting and draining removes excess water for salads.
Cucumber.waste: Quick-pickle leftover chunks in vinegar, sugar and salt, or grate them into tzatziki or raita, squeezing out excess water first.

Florence fennel.about: Florence fennel is a bulb with layers of crisp, juicy flesh and a sweet aniseed flavour. Raw fennel is fresh and crunchy, and cooking mellows it to sweet and soft. British-grown bulbs are available from early summer into autumn.
Florence fennel.choose: Choose firm, white, rounded bulbs with no browning, and if fronds are attached they should be bright and fresh.
Florence fennel.store: Keep in the fridge for up to a week.
Florence fennel.prep: Slice thinly and serve raw in salads, or roast, braise or grill. It goes very well with fish and pork.
Florence fennel.waste: Chop the feathery fronds over salads or fish like dill, and slice the tougher stalks into stock or slow braises.

French beans.about: French beans are slender green beans eaten pod and all, crisp and tender with a clean, grassy flavour. British crops run through summer, alongside extra-fine beans and yellow wax beans. Home-grown beans picked young are far more tender than the air-freighted packs sold the rest of the year, and they cook in minutes.
French beans.choose: Choose firm, bright beans that snap cleanly and have no brown spots.
French beans.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three or four days.
French beans.prep: Top the stalk end and boil or steam for a few minutes until just tender, then dress while warm. They are good in salade niçoise and with garlic butter.
French beans.waste: Blanch and freeze any surplus, and use up tired beans in a slow-cooked tomato stew where crispness does not matter.

Runner beans.about: Runner beans are long, flat beans with a robust, beany flavour and a bit of crunch. They are a traditional British allotment crop, often grown up cane wigwams, and they crop heavily from late summer. Young beans are the most tender.
Runner beans.choose: Choose bright green beans that snap cleanly when bent, avoiding any that are bulging, stringy or limp.
Runner beans.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three or four days.
Runner beans.prep: String the sides with a peeler or knife and slice diagonally, then boil or steam until tender. They suit butter, tomatoes and slow-cooked dishes.
Runner beans.caution: Raw runner beans contain lectins that can cause stomach upset, so always cook them thoroughly before eating.
Runner beans.waste: Slice and freeze surplus beans after a quick blanch, or turn a glut into runner bean chutney.

Borlotti beans.about: Borlotti beans grow in striking pink and cream speckled pods, and the fresh beans inside are creamy and nutty when cooked. Fresh beans appear briefly in late summer and early autumn, and they cook far more quickly than dried. The mottled colour fades to brown as they cook.
Borlotti beans.choose: Choose plump, firm pods with bright markings that are slightly leathery, which shows the beans inside are fully formed.
Borlotti beans.store: Keep in the pod in the fridge for up to five days, or pod and freeze.
Borlotti beans.prep: Pod and simmer in water with garlic, sage and olive oil for 20 to 30 minutes until creamy. They are good in soups, stews and salads.
Borlotti beans.caution: Raw borlotti beans contain lectins that can make you ill, so always cook them fully before eating.
Borlotti beans.waste: Keep the cooking liquid from fresh or dried beans, as it adds body to soups and stews, and freeze cooked beans in their liquid.

Wet garlic.about: Wet garlic is garlic that has been harvested young, before the bulb dries. It is mild and sweet, and the whole plant, from bulb to soft stem, can be used. It is only available briefly in early summer, with much British wet garlic coming from the Isle of Wight.
Wet garlic.choose: Choose firm, fresh bulbs with white, moist skins and green stems.
Wet garlic.store: Keep in the fridge and use within a week.
Wet garlic.prep: Slice the whole head and stem like a leek, then soften in butter for soups and risottos, or roast whole and squeeze out the sweet flesh. It is also good raw in salads.
Wet garlic.waste: Use the whole thing, including the green stems, sliced into dishes like a leek, and chop any trimmings into butter or oil for cooking.

Garlic.about: Dried British garlic is harvested in midsummer, then cured and kept through the autumn and winter. It is pungent raw and becomes sweet and mellow when cooked slowly or roasted. The Isle of Wight is the best-known British growing area, and hardneck varieties grown there often have fewer, larger cloves with a stronger flavour than imported garlic.
Garlic.choose: Choose firm, heavy bulbs with tight, dry skin and no green shoots or soft cloves.
Garlic.store: Store in a cool, dry, airy place for several months, away from the fridge.
Garlic.prep: Peel and crush or slice for frying, or roast whole until soft. Remove any green shoot, which can be bitter.
Garlic.waste: Add papery skins and odd ends to the stock bag, and roast whole heads that are starting to sprout, then squeeze the soft cloves into sauces.

Jerusalem artichokes.about: Jerusalem artichokes are knobbly tubers of a type of sunflower, with a sweet, nutty flavour reminiscent of globe artichokes. They are a British winter crop and make excellent soups and roasts, turning creamy inside and crisp at the edges. They contain inulin, which some people find hard to digest, so start with modest portions.
Jerusalem artichokes.choose: Choose firm, smooth tubers with as few knobbles as possible to make peeling easier.
Jerusalem artichokes.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge and use within two weeks.
Jerusalem artichokes.prep: Scrub well, or peel and drop into lemony water to stop browning, then roast, sauté or make into a velvety soup. They also make good crisps.
Jerusalem artichokes.waste: Scrub rather than peel, as the skins are thin and edible, and roast leftover small knobbly bits for crisps or soup.

Kale.about: Kale is a hardy winter brassica with crinkled leaves and a robust, slightly bitter flavour that sweetens after frost. Curly green kale is the most common, alongside red and Russian varieties. It is a dependable British green through the coldest months.
Kale.choose: Choose crisp, deeply coloured leaves without yellowing, and avoid any that smell strongly of cabbage.
Kale.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within four or five days.
Kale.prep: Strip the leaves from the tough stalks, then wilt, stir-fry or roast into crisps. It is good in soups and stews and with beans.
Kale.waste: Strip the leaves, then slice the tough stalks thinly and fry or simmer them in soups, or blitz them into pesto.

Cavolo nero.about: Cavolo nero, or Tuscan kale, has long, dark, bubbly leaves and a rich, earthy flavour. It is sweeter and more tender than curly kale, and it grows well in Britain through autumn and winter. It is essential in ribollita, the Tuscan bread and bean soup.
Cavolo nero.choose: Choose dark, glossy, crisp leaves without yellowing or limpness.
Cavolo nero.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within five days.
Cavolo nero.prep: Strip the leaves from the stalks, then blanch, sauté or add to soups and stews. It can also be blitzed into a pesto or sauce for pasta.
Cavolo nero.waste: Finely chop the tough central ribs and cook them a few minutes longer than the leaves, or blend the leftovers into a green pesto.

Kalettes.about: Kalettes are a British-bred cross between kale and Brussels sprouts, producing small, frilly green and purple rosettes. They have a mild, nutty flavour and are sweeter than both their parents. They cook quickly and are available through winter.
Kalettes.choose: Choose bright, crisp kalettes with no yellowing or wilting.
Kalettes.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within four or five days.
Kalettes.prep: Roast, stir-fry or steam for a few minutes so they keep some bite. They suit garlic, chilli and lemon.
Kalettes.waste: Roast any loose or wilted kalettes until crisp, and add leftover cooked ones to bubble and squeak or a frittata.

Kohlrabi.about: Kohlrabi is a bulbous brassica with a sweet, mild flavour similar to broccoli stalks and a crisp texture. It is available in green and purple varieties. It grows well in Britain from summer into autumn and is good raw or cooked.
Kohlrabi.choose: Choose small to medium bulbs that feel heavy and firm, with smooth skin and fresh leaves.
Kohlrabi.store: Remove the leaves (cook them like spinach) and keep the bulb in the fridge for up to two weeks.
Kohlrabi.prep: Peel and slice or grate raw into salads and slaws, or roast, stir-fry or add to stews. Larger bulbs can be woody.
Kohlrabi.waste: Cook the young leaves like kale and grate leftover bulb into slaw, peeling only the tough outer layer.

Leeks.about: Leeks are long, mild members of the onion family with a sweet flavour when cooked gently. They are a British winter staple and the national emblem of Wales. They are in season from late summer through to spring.
Leeks.choose: Choose firm, straight leeks with tightly wrapped leaves and plenty of white, avoiding any that look slimy or dry.
Leeks.store: Keep in the fridge for up to a week.
Leeks.prep: Trim and wash well between the layers to remove grit, then sweat in butter, add to soups and pies, or braise. Young leeks are good grilled.
Leeks.waste: Wash the dark green tops well and use them in stock, soups or slow-cooked dishes, where they soften nicely.

Lettuce.about: British lettuce ranges from soft, round butterhead to crisp Little Gem, cos and frilly loose-leaf types. It is at its best in early summer, when leaves are tender and sweet. Freshly picked lettuce has far more flavour than bagged salad.
Lettuce.choose: Choose crisp, bright heads with no wilting, browning or slimy leaves.
Lettuce.store: Wrap in damp paper or keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three or four days.
Lettuce.prep: Wash and dry thoroughly before dressing at the last minute. Little Gem and cos are also good grilled or braised with peas.
Lettuce.waste: Wilt tired lettuce into soups with peas, or braise the hearts, rather than throwing away leaves that are past their crisp best.

Lamb's lettuce.about: Lamb's lettuce, also called corn salad or mâche, has small, rounded leaves with a mild, nutty flavour and soft texture. It grows through the colder months, making it one of the few British salad leaves available in winter. It is good on its own or mixed with stronger leaves.
Lamb's lettuce.choose: Choose small, bright green rosettes with no wilting or yellowing.
Lamb's lettuce.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within two or three days.
Lamb's lettuce.prep: Wash carefully to remove grit, then dress lightly just before serving. It suits beetroot, walnuts and soft cheeses.
Lamb's lettuce.waste: Revive slightly wilted leaves in iced water, and stir any that are past it into soups or blitz them into a green sauce.

Mizuna & mustard greens.about: Mizuna and mustard greens are oriental salad leaves with a peppery, mustardy flavour. Mizuna has feathery, mild leaves, while red mustard is hotter. They grow well in British autumn and winter, providing fresh salad leaves through the cooler months.
Mizuna & mustard greens.choose: Choose crisp, fresh leaves with no wilting or yellowing.
Mizuna & mustard greens.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three days.
Mizuna & mustard greens.prep: Use raw in mixed salads, or wilt briefly in stir-fries and soups. They suit Asian dressings and rich meats.
Mizuna & mustard greens.waste: Wilt older or tougher leaves into stir-fries, soups or noodles, where their peppery flavour mellows with cooking.

Rocket.about: Rocket has a peppery, nutty flavour and tender leaves that wake up a plate of salad. Wild rocket is more pungent than salad rocket and has narrower, deeply cut leaves. British-grown rocket is available from spring to autumn, with summer crops the most plentiful, and fresh bunches have more bite than bagged leaves.
Rocket.choose: Choose bright, perky leaves with no yellowing or sliminess.
Rocket.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within two or three days.
Rocket.prep: Use raw in salads and sandwiches, or scatter over pizza and pasta at the end. It suits parmesan, lemon and cured meats.
Rocket.waste: Blitz rocket that is starting to wilt into a pesto with nuts, cheese and oil, which keeps in the fridge or freezes well.

Watercress.about: Watercress is a peppery, mineral-rich leaf grown in clear chalk-stream beds. Hampshire and Dorset are the main British growing areas, and Alresford's Watercress Line railway was named after the trade. It is at its best in spring and early summer.
Watercress.choose: Choose dark green, crisp leaves with no yellowing or wilting.
Watercress.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge, or stand stems in water, and use within two or three days.
Watercress.prep: Use raw in salads and sandwiches, or blend into a vivid green soup. It suits rich fish and meat, cutting through fat.
Watercress.waste: Use the thicker stalks in soup with potato, and blend leftover leaves into a sauce for fish or a dressing.

Pak choi.about: Pak choi is a Chinese cabbage with crisp white stems and tender, dark green leaves. It has a mild, sweet flavour and juicy texture. It is grown in Britain from late spring to autumn, and baby pak choi is often sold whole.
Pak choi.choose: Choose firm, crisp heads with bright green leaves and no yellowing or brown spots.
Pak choi.store: Keep in the fridge and use within three or four days.
Pak choi.prep: Halve or quarter lengthways and wash well, then stir-fry, steam or braise briefly. It suits ginger, garlic and soy.
Pak choi.waste: Slice the white stems and cook them before the leaves, and add any wilted heads to soups or noodle broths.

Mangetout.about: Mangetout, French for 'eat everything', are flat pea pods eaten whole before the peas inside develop. They are crisp, sweet and fresh tasting, with a clean green flavour. British crops are available through summer, and freshly picked pods are noticeably sweeter and crunchier than the imported packs found in supermarkets the rest of the year.
Mangetout.choose: Choose bright, flat pods that snap cleanly, with no yellowing or limpness.
Mangetout.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three days.
Mangetout.prep: Top and tail, removing any string, then stir-fry or blanch briefly, or eat raw. They suit Asian flavours and summer salads.
Mangetout.waste: Snip off just the stalk end rather than trimming heavily, and stir any limp mangetout into stir-fries or noodle dishes.

Sugar snap peas.about: Sugar snap peas are plump, edible pea pods with sweet, juicy peas inside, a cross between mangetout and garden peas. They are crunchier and sweeter than mangetout. British crops run through summer, and like all peas they lose sweetness after picking, so local pods eaten raw or barely cooked are at their best.
Sugar snap peas.choose: Choose firm, bright green pods that snap cleanly when bent.
Sugar snap peas.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three days.
Sugar snap peas.prep: Top and tail, removing the string, then eat raw, blanch briefly or stir-fry. They suit mint, sesame and lemon.
Sugar snap peas.waste: Pull off the strings and eat the whole pod, and blanch and freeze any surplus or use it in stir-fries.

Peas.about: Fresh peas are one of the great tastes of the British summer, sweet and tender when picked young. Their sugars turn to starch quickly after picking, so eat them as soon as possible. Most British peas are frozen within hours of harvest, but fresh pods appear at markets in early summer.
Peas.choose: Choose bright green, plump pods that feel full and squeak when rubbed together.
Peas.store: Keep in the pod in the fridge and eat within a day or two.
Peas.prep: Pod just before cooking and boil briefly, or eat raw. They suit mint, butter and bacon, and make good soups and risottos.
Peas.waste: Simmer the empty pods with onion and herbs for a sweet stock for soup or risotto, or blend the tenderest pods into soup and sieve it.

Marrow.about: Marrows are courgettes left to grow large, with mild flesh and tougher skin. They have a gentle flavour that takes on other ingredients well, which makes them good for stuffing and chutney. They are a traditional British vegetable, a fixture of village shows and allotment gluts from late summer into autumn, and usually very cheap.
Marrow.choose: Choose medium marrows with firm, unblemished skin; very large ones can be watery and seedy.
Marrow.store: Keep in a cool place for a week or two.
Marrow.prep: Peel and remove the seeds, then stuff and bake, make into chutney, or cook into soups and curries. It suits strong flavours.
Marrow.waste: Use the softest seeds with the flesh, and turn a large marrow into chutney or jam, or stuff and bake it.

Onions.about: Onions are a staple of British cooking, pungent raw and sweet when cooked slowly. Home-grown onions are harvested in late summer, dried in the field or in stores, and kept through the winter, with Lincolnshire and East Anglia the main growing areas. They form the base of countless soups, stews and sauces.
Onions.choose: Choose firm, heavy onions with dry, papery skin and no soft spots or green shoots.
Onions.store: Store in a cool, dry, dark place for several months, away from potatoes.
Onions.prep: Peel and slice or chop, then sweat gently in butter or oil for stews and soups, or roast or caramelise slowly. Raw onion suits salads and pickles.
Onions.waste: Save skins and ends for the stock bag, as the skins add a deep colour, and fry up leftover halves for a pan of caramelised onions.

Red onions.about: Red onions are milder and sweeter than brown onions, with a deep purple skin and purple-ringed flesh. They are harvested in late summer and stored through the winter, so British ones are available for most of the cold months. They are good raw in salads and quick pickles, and they roast to a soft, jammy sweetness.
Red onions.choose: Choose firm onions with dry, shiny skin and no soft spots or shoots.
Red onions.store: Store in a cool, dry, dark place for several months.
Red onions.prep: Slice thinly and soak in cold water or lemon juice to soften for salads, or roast, pickle or make into marmalade. They suit roasted vegetables and grilled meats.
Red onions.waste: Quick-pickle leftover halves in vinegar, sugar and salt, and add the skins and ends to the stock bag.

Shallots.about: Shallots are small, clustered alliums with a sweeter, more delicate flavour than onions. Banana shallots are long and easy to peel. They are harvested in summer and stored through winter, and they are key to many French sauces.
Shallots.choose: Choose firm, dry shallots with no soft spots, shoots or mould.
Shallots.store: Store in a cool, dry, dark place for several months.
Shallots.prep: Peel and chop finely for dressings and sauces, or roast or braise whole. They suit red wine, vinegar and game.
Shallots.waste: Add the peel and trimmings to stock, and slice leftover shallots thinly and fry them until crisp for a topping that keeps in a jar.

Spring onions.about: Spring onions are young onions harvested before the bulb forms, with a mild, fresh flavour and crisp texture. Both the white and green parts can be used, raw or cooked. British spring onions are available from spring to late summer, and fresh bunches with perky tops are much more flavourful than tired, limp ones.
Spring onions.choose: Choose firm, bright onions with crisp green tops and white bulbs.
Spring onions.store: Keep in the fridge and use within a week.
Spring onions.prep: Trim the roots and any limp tops, then slice into salads, stir-fries and sauces. They can also be grilled whole.
Spring onions.waste: Use the green tops as well as the white, and stand the trimmed roots in water to regrow a few more green shoots.

Parsnips.about: Parsnips are sweet, nutty roots that get sweeter after frost, when cold converts some of their starch into sugar. They are a classic British winter vegetable and an essential part of a roast dinner. They were used as a sweetener in Britain before sugar was widely available, and they work well in cakes too.
Parsnips.choose: Choose firm, smooth, medium parsnips; very large ones can have a woody core.
Parsnips.store: Keep in the fridge for two to three weeks.
Parsnips.prep: Peel and roast with honey or maple, add to stews, mash, or make into soup. Remove the woody core from large roots.
Parsnips.waste: Scrub rather than peel, and roast any peelings with oil and salt until crisp for a snack.

Peppers.about: Sweet peppers are grown in British glasshouses, including in the Lea Valley on London's northern edge, and come into their own in late summer. Green ones are simply unripe and taste grassy, while red, yellow and orange peppers are sweeter and fruitier. Home-grown ones travel less and are often picked riper than imports.
Peppers.choose: Pick glossy, firm peppers that feel heavy for their size, with a green, fresh-looking stalk and no soft or wrinkled patches.
Peppers.store: Keep them whole in the salad drawer of the fridge, where they last about a week.
Peppers.prep: Halve, remove the seeds and white pith, then roast, grill or char over a gas flame until blackened, peel and dress with oil. They are also good raw in salads or slow-cooked with onions and tomatoes into peperonata.
Peppers.waste: Roast soft or wrinkled peppers, then peel and store them in oil in the fridge, or blend them into a sauce or dip.

Chillies.about: British growers raise chillies under glass from midsummer, from mild jalapeños to the fierce Dorset Naga, developed by a grower in Dorset. Each variety has its own fruitiness as well as heat, which mostly sits in the pale pith and seeds. Late summer brings the widest choice of fresh UK chillies.
Chillies.choose: Choose shiny, firm, smooth chillies with fresh green stalks, and ask the stallholder how hot each variety is.
Chillies.store: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge for one to two weeks, or freeze whole and grate from frozen.
Chillies.prep: Remove the seeds and pith to tame the heat, then slice into salsas, stir-fries and dressings, or char whole on the grill. Wash your hands well afterwards and keep them away from your eyes.
Chillies.waste: Freeze spare chillies whole to grate from frozen, or dry them on a sunny windowsill and crumble them into dishes.

Jersey Royal potatoes.about: Jersey Royals are small kidney-shaped new potatoes grown only on Jersey and protected by PDO status. Many are planted on steep south-facing slopes called côtils and fed with vraic, a local seaweed. They have papery skins and a sweet, nutty, slightly earthy flavour that is at its best in May and June.
Jersey Royal potatoes.choose: Look for small, firm potatoes with skins that flake off when rubbed with a thumb, ideally with a little soil still on them.
Jersey Royal potatoes.store: Keep in a paper bag in a cool, dark place and use within three or four days, as they lose flavour quickly.
Jersey Royal potatoes.prep: Rinse or scrub gently without peeling, boil in salted water until just tender, and toss with butter and sea salt. Leftovers are good cold in salads with herbs.
Jersey Royal potatoes.waste: Keep the thin skins on, and use leftover cooked potatoes in a salad, hash or frittata, cutting away any green patches first.

New potatoes.about: New potatoes are early varieties lifted while young, so their skins are thin and their flesh waxy and sweet. Charlotte, Anya and the knobbly Pink Fir Apple are good salad types to look out for. Freshly dug British new potatoes have a clean, earthy flavour that fades the longer they are stored.
New potatoes.choose: Choose firm, unblemished potatoes with skins that rub off easily, and avoid any that are green, soft or sprouting.
New potatoes.store: Keep in a paper bag in a cool, dark place, away from onions, and use within a week.
New potatoes.prep: Scrub rather than peel, then boil, steam or roast whole. They hold their shape well in potato salads, warm or cold.
New potatoes.waste: Cook them in their skins, and use leftovers in potato salad, hash or a Spanish omelette, but cut away any green or sprouting parts.

Maincrop potatoes.about: Maincrop potatoes are lifted in autumn once the skins have set, then stored to see us through winter. Maris Piper and King Edward are floury and good for chips, roasties and mash, while waxier types such as Désirée hold together in stews. Their fuller, starchier flavour suits cold-weather cooking.
Maincrop potatoes.choose: Buy firm, dry potatoes with no green patches, sprouts, cuts or soft spots, and pick the variety to suit the dish.
Maincrop potatoes.store: Store unwashed in a paper or hessian sack in a cool, dark, airy place, where they keep for several weeks.
Maincrop potatoes.prep: Peel or scrub, then roast, mash, bake, chip or add to stews; for crisp roast potatoes, parboil floury ones, rough up the edges and roast in very hot fat.
Maincrop potatoes.waste: Roast clean peelings until crisp for a snack and use leftover mash in fishcakes or bubble and squeak, but discard any green skin or sprouts.

Radishes.about: Radishes are quick-growing roots with crisp, juicy flesh and a peppery bite that grows hotter as the summer warms. The long red and white French Breakfast type is a favourite at British markets in spring. Early-season radishes are the mildest and crunchiest, and their leaves are edible too.
Radishes.choose: Look for firm, smooth radishes with bright, perky leaves, and pass over any that feel spongy or are split.
Radishes.store: Cut off the leaves, then keep the roots in a container in the fridge for up to a week; use the leaves within a day.
Radishes.prep: Eat raw with soft butter and sea salt, slice into salads, or halve and roast or braise briefly in butter. The leaves can be wilted like spinach or blended into pesto.
Radishes.waste: Use fresh, unwilted radish leaves in soup or pesto, or sauté them with butter, and roast any slightly soft radishes.

Salsify.about: Salsify is a long, thin root with a mild, nutty, slightly sweet flavour that some compare to oysters or artichoke. The black-skinned kind, strictly called scorzonera, is the one most often sold. It is an old-fashioned British winter vegetable, now found mainly at good greengrocers and farmers' markets from autumn into winter.
Salsify.choose: Choose firm, straight, fairly thick roots that snap rather than bend, without soft or shrivelled ends.
Salsify.store: Wrap in paper and keep in the fridge salad drawer for up to a week.
Salsify.prep: Peel with gloves on as the sap is sticky, dropping pieces straight into water with lemon juice to stop them browning. Boil or steam until tender, then fry in butter, add to gratins or serve with game.
Salsify.waste: Scrub and cook it in its skin before peeling, which saves flesh, and add leftover cooked salsify to gratins or soups.

Samphire.about: Marsh samphire, also called glasswort, grows on tidal salt marshes such as those on the north Norfolk coast. It has crisp, juicy, jointed green stems and a fresh, salty taste of the sea. It is only around for a few weeks in summer, which is the time to eat it with fish and shellfish.
Samphire.choose: Choose bright green, crisp, springy stems, avoiding any that look slimy, yellowing or woody at the base.
Samphire.store: Wrap in damp kitchen paper in the fridge and use within three or four days.
Samphire.prep: Rinse well, pick off any tough stalks, then blanch or steam for a minute or two and toss in butter. It is salty already, so do not add salt.
Samphire.waste: Use the tender tips raw or lightly steamed, and add the slightly woody lower stems to fish stock, where they add a salty, sea flavour.

Spinach.about: Spinach has tender dark green leaves with a soft, mineral flavour, mild when young and stronger as the leaves mature. UK-grown spinach is at its sweetest in spring before hot weather makes it bolt. It cooks down dramatically, so a big bag makes a modest pile.
Spinach.choose: Pick perky, deep green leaves with no yellowing, slime or wilting, and allow about 250g raw per person for cooking.
Spinach.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within two or three days.
Spinach.prep: Wash well in plenty of water to remove grit and pull out any tough stalks. Eat young leaves raw, or wilt in a pan with a little butter or oil and squeeze out the excess water before adding to pies, curries, eggs or gratins.
Spinach.waste: Wilt spinach that is past its best into soups, curries or omelettes, or blanch and freeze it in portions.

Swede.about: Swede is a large root with purple-tinged skin and sweet, peppery orange flesh, related to the turnip. In Scotland it is the 'neeps' served with haggis on Burns Night, and it goes into the traditional Cornish pasty. Frost sweetens it, so it is best in the depths of winter.
Swede.choose: Choose a heavy, firm swede with smooth skin and no soft patches or cracks; smaller ones tend to be sweeter.
Swede.store: Keep it in a cool, dark place or the fridge, where it lasts two to three weeks.
Swede.prep: Peel thickly with a sturdy knife, chop into chunks, then boil and mash with butter and lots of black pepper, or roast, or add to stews and pasties.
Swede.waste: Mash leftover swede with carrot or potato and fry it into cakes, and add the peelings to the stock bag.

Sweetcorn.about: Sweetcorn is picked when the kernels are full of sugary milk, and that sugar starts turning to starch from the moment the cob is cut. English cobs are at their best in late summer, ideally from a farm shop or market where they were picked that day. Fresh corn tastes sweet, juicy and buttery.
Sweetcorn.choose: Choose cobs with tight green husks and moist, light brown silk, and check the kernels are plump and pop with milky juice when pressed.
Sweetcorn.store: Eat it the day you buy it if you can; otherwise keep in the husk in the fridge for a day or two.
Sweetcorn.prep: Strip off the husk and silk, then boil for three to four minutes, or grill or barbecue until charred in places. Slice the kernels off for fritters, salsas, soups and chowders.
Sweetcorn.waste: Simmer the stripped cobs with onion and water for a sweet stock that makes a good chowder or soup base.

Tomatoes.about: British tomatoes are mostly grown under glass, with notable growers on the Isle of Wight and in the Lea Valley. They range from sweet cherry tomatoes to large beefsteaks, and they are at their juiciest and most fragrant in high summer. Sun-ripened, home-grown fruit has a depth of flavour that winter imports lack.
Tomatoes.choose: Choose tomatoes that smell of their green vines, feel heavy and give slightly when pressed, with rich, even colour.
Tomatoes.store: Keep at room temperature out of direct sun and eat within a few days; the fridge dulls their flavour and texture.
Tomatoes.prep: Slice and salt raw tomatoes a few minutes before dressing them with oil, or roast, grill or slow-cook into sauces. Riper, softer ones are best for cooking.
Tomatoes.waste: Roast soft or split tomatoes for sauce or soup and freeze it, but do not eat the leaves or green stalks.

Heritage tomatoes.about: Heritage or heirloom tomatoes are older, open-pollinated varieties grown for flavour over uniform looks. Look out for the pink Brandywine, dark Black Krim, striped Green Zebra and ribbed Marmande. They vary from sweet to sharp and smoky, and British-grown ones are at their best in late summer.
Heritage tomatoes.choose: Pick fragrant tomatoes that feel heavy and give slightly; odd shapes and small cracks at the shoulders are normal and fine.
Heritage tomatoes.store: Keep at room temperature out of direct sun and eat within two or three days.
Heritage tomatoes.prep: Slice a mix of colours, season with salt, then dress simply with good olive oil. They are best raw, as cooking loses the differences between varieties.
Heritage tomatoes.waste: Use the core and seedy pulp in sauces, soups or dressings, and slow-roast any overripe ones, discarding leaves and green stalks.

Turnips.about: Turnips have white flesh with a crisp, peppery, slightly sweet flavour. Small summer turnips, often white with a purple top, are tender enough to eat raw, while larger winter ones are earthier and best cooked. Their leafy tops, sold as turnip tops or greens, are good to eat too.
Turnips.choose: Choose small to medium turnips that feel heavy and firm, with smooth skin and fresh leaves if still attached.
Turnips.store: Remove the tops and keep the roots in the fridge for one to two weeks; use the greens within two days.
Turnips.prep: Peel larger ones, but baby turnips need only a scrub. Glaze in butter with a little sugar and stock, roast alongside meat, or add to braises and soups.
Turnips.waste: Cook the young turnip tops like spring greens, and roast or mash any leftover roots.

Bramley apples.about: The Bramley is Britain's classic cooking apple, grown from a pip planted in Southwell, Nottinghamshire, in the early 1800s. It is large, green and very sharp, and it cooks down to a fluffy purée that holds its tang. Bramleys are picked in autumn and stored to last the whole year.
Bramley apples.choose: Choose firm, heavy apples with no bruises or soft spots; a slight red blush is fine.
Bramley apples.store: Keep in a cool, dark place or the fridge, where they last several weeks.
Bramley apples.prep: Peel, core and slice, then stew with a little sugar for crumbles, pies and apple sauce, or bake whole stuffed with dried fruit. They also add sharpness to braised red cabbage and roast pork.
Bramley apples.waste: Simmer Bramley peels and cores with water and sugar for a quick jelly, or cover them with water and a little sugar to ferment into apple scrap vinegar.

Eating apples.about: Britain grows hundreds of apple varieties, from the early Discovery in August to the aromatic Cox's Orange Pippin and the nutty Egremont Russet in autumn. Kent, Herefordshire and Somerset are major apple counties. British apples are stored through winter and spring, but they are crispest and most varied straight after the autumn harvest.
Eating apples.choose: Choose firm apples with no bruises or wrinkled skin, and try unfamiliar varieties at farmers' markets, where you can often taste before buying.
Eating apples.store: Keep them in the fridge, or a cool dark place, where crisp varieties last several weeks.
Eating apples.prep: Eat raw with cheese or sliced into salads, or use firmer varieties for tarts, baking and frying with pork. Toss cut slices in lemon juice to stop browning.
Eating apples.waste: Save cores and peels in the freezer for jelly or scrap vinegar, and grate soft, wrinkly apples into porridge, flapjacks or cake batter.

Pears.about: British pears are harvested in late summer and autumn, with Conference the main variety and Comice prized for its buttery, juicy flesh. Ripe pears are sweet and fragrant with a soft, melting texture. Like apples, they are stored into spring, but they are at their best in autumn.
Pears.choose: Pears ripen from the inside, so press gently near the stalk: a little give means it is ripe, and buy firmer ones if you want to cook them.
Pears.store: Ripen at room temperature, then keep in the fridge for a few days once ready.
Pears.prep: Eat ripe pears raw with cheese or in salads, or poach firmer ones in wine or syrup, bake in tarts and crumbles, or roast alongside game.
Pears.waste: Poach overripe or bruised pears into a compote for porridge, and simmer the peels and cores with sugar and spices to make a light syrup for drinks.

Quince.about: Quince is a large, golden, often knobbly fruit related to apples and pears, too hard and astringent to eat raw. Long, slow cooking turns its pale flesh pink or amber and brings out a perfumed, honeyed flavour. British-grown quinces turn up briefly in autumn, often from garden trees, and are the base of Spanish membrillo.
Quince.choose: Choose fragrant, yellow, unbruised fruit; a grey fuzz on the skin is normal and rubs off.
Quince.store: Keep in a cool place for two to three weeks, away from other fruit as their strong scent spreads.
Quince.prep: Rub off the fuzz, then peel and core with a heavy knife, as the flesh is very hard. Poach slowly in syrup, bake, add a few slices to apple pies, or cook into jelly or membrillo.
Quince.waste: Boil quince peels and cores in water to make a pectin-rich, rosy liquid you can strain and use as the base for quince jelly.

Medlars.about: Medlars are small, russet-brown fruit with an open, crown-like end, grown in Britain since medieval times. They are hard and astringent when picked and must be 'bletted', left until soft and brown inside. Bletted medlars taste of dates, toffee and baked apple, and make a fine jelly to eat with game or cheese.
Medlars.choose: Buy firm, undamaged fruit and blet them at home, or choose ones already soft and brown if you want to use them straight away.
Medlars.store: Blet on a tray in a cool place, eye down and not touching, for two to three weeks until soft, then use within a few days.
Medlars.prep: Scoop the soft pulp from bletted fruit and eat it as it is, or cook whole medlars with water and sugar to make jelly or medlar cheese.
Medlars.waste: Once bletted, push the soft flesh through a sieve to leave the skins and seeds behind, then use the purée for medlar cheese or a spiced compote.

Plums.about: British plums run from July to October, with the red and gold Victoria, first found in Sussex in the 1840s, the best known. The Vale of Evesham in Worcestershire is the traditional plum country. Ripe plums are juicy and sweet with a tart skin, and cooking brings out their colour and sharpness.
Plums.choose: Choose plums that give slightly when pressed, with a natural dusty bloom and no splits or wet patches.
Plums.store: Ripen firm ones at room temperature, then keep in the fridge for three or four days.
Plums.prep: Eat ripe plums raw, or halve, stone and roast with a little sugar and spice, bake into crumbles and cakes, or cook into jam and sauces for duck and pork.
Plums.waste: Stew soft or split plums into a compote that freezes well, and use the leftover juice from stewing as a cordial or to soak a sponge.

Damsons.about: Damsons are small, dark blue-black plums with a dusty bloom and intensely sharp, tannic flesh that is too sour to eat raw. Cooking with sugar brings out a deep, spicy plum flavour. The Lyth Valley in Cumbria is famous for them, and the short early-autumn season is the time for damson jam, cheese and gin.
Damsons.choose: Choose firm but not rock-hard fruit with an intact bloom and no splits, and buy plenty, as the season is short.
Damsons.store: Keep in the fridge for up to a week, or freeze whole for jams and gin later.
Damsons.prep: Cook whole with sugar and a splash of water, then sieve or pick out the stones once soft. Use for crumbles, jam, fruit cheese, sauces for game and duck, or steep in gin.
Damsons.waste: Cook damsons whole and skim the stones out as they rise, then use any leftover pulp from jelly-making in a crumble or fruit leather.

Greengages.about: Greengages are small, round, green or yellow-green plums with honeyed, aromatic flesh, often thought the finest dessert plums. The English name comes from the Gage family, who brought the French Reine Claude to England in the 18th century. Their season is brief, so look for them in August.
Greengages.choose: Choose fruit that is slightly soft with a yellow tinge or light russet speckles, which signal sweetness, and avoid hard, bright green ones.
Greengages.store: Eat ripe greengages within a day or two, keeping them in the fridge if needed.
Greengages.prep: Eat ripe ones raw, or halve and bake in tarts, poach lightly, or make jam, which keeps their honey flavour well.
Greengages.waste: Turn overripe greengages into a quick jam or compote, or halve, stone and freeze them on a tray to use in crumbles later.

Cherries.about: Kent has been England's cherry country for centuries, and new dwarf orchards have revived British growing in recent decades. Sweet cherries are juicy and rich, from dark red to pale blushed varieties. The English season is short and centred on July, so it is worth seeking out home-grown fruit.
Cherries.choose: Choose plump, shiny, firm cherries with green, flexible stalks, avoiding any that are split, soft or have dried stems.
Cherries.store: Keep unwashed in the fridge and eat within three to five days, rinsing just before eating.
Cherries.prep: Eat raw by the handful, or stone them for clafoutis, pies, compotes and sauces to serve with duck. A cherry stoner makes the job much quicker.
Cherries.waste: Stone and freeze overripe cherries for compotes and smoothies, and throw the stones away rather than cracking them, as the kernels are not safe to eat.

Strawberries.about: British strawberries run from late spring into autumn, but June and July bring the most fragrant fruit and the Wimbledon tradition of strawberries and cream. Elsanta is common in shops, while varieties such as Cambridge Favourite and Malling Centenary are worth seeking out. Home-grown fruit picked ripe has the best scent and sweetness.
Strawberries.choose: Choose fragrant, glossy berries that are red right up to the green hull, and check the bottom of the punnet for mould or juice.
Strawberries.store: Keep unwashed in the fridge for one to two days, and bring back to room temperature before eating for the best flavour.
Strawberries.prep: Rinse just before hulling, then eat raw with cream, slice into salads, macerate with sugar and a little balsamic, or make jam.
Strawberries.waste: Steep the green tops in water or cider vinegar for a lightly fruity drink or dressing, and blitz soft strawberries into a sauce or freeze them for smoothies.

Raspberries.about: Scotland, especially Tayside around Blairgowrie, has a long tradition of raspberry growing, and cooler summers there give the fruit good flavour. Raspberries are soft, fragrant and sweet-sharp. Summer varieties fruit in July and August, then autumn-fruiting types carry the season on into October.
Raspberries.choose: Choose dry, plump, evenly coloured berries and check the punnet for crushed or mouldy fruit at the bottom.
Raspberries.store: Spread out on a plate in the fridge and eat within a day or two; they also freeze well.
Raspberries.prep: Avoid washing if you can. Eat raw with cream, add to summer puddings and pavlovas, sieve into a coulis, or make cranachan with toasted oats, whisky, honey and cream.
Raspberries.waste: Sieve squashed or soft raspberries into a coulis that freezes well in ice cube trays, ready for yoghurt, ice cream or drinks.

Blackberries.about: Blackberries grow wild in hedgerows all over Britain and are also cultivated in larger, thornless varieties. They are sweet, sharp and winey when fully ripe. Folklore says not to pick them after Michaelmas, when the devil is said to spoil them, and late berries do tend to be watery and mouldy.
Blackberries.choose: Pick or buy plump, glossy, fully black berries that come away easily; avoid red ones, and pick away from busy roadsides.
Blackberries.store: Keep unwashed in a single layer in the fridge for a day or two, or freeze on a tray.
Blackberries.prep: Rinse gently just before use. Eat raw, or bake with apples in crumbles and pies, cook into jam and jelly, or make a sauce for game.
Blackberries.waste: Cook soft or mixed-quality blackberries into a compote or jelly, and use the seedy pulp left in the jelly bag to flavour a crumble or vinegar.

Blackcurrants.about: Blackcurrants are small, intensely sharp berries with a deep, musky flavour, packed with vitamin C. Most British blackcurrants go into cordials, but fresh ones turn up in July and August at markets and pick-your-own farms. Many modern varieties were bred in Scotland and carry the prefix 'Ben'.
Blackcurrants.choose: Choose firm, shiny, plump berries still on their strings, with no shrivelled or mouldy fruit.
Blackcurrants.store: Keep in the fridge for up to five days, or strip from the stalks and freeze.
Blackcurrants.prep: Strip the berries from the stalks with a fork, then cook with sugar for jams, compotes, fools, sorbets and summer pudding. The leaves can be used to flavour custards and syrups.
Blackcurrants.waste: Infuse a few young blackcurrant leaves in cream or syrup for a fragrant flavour, and use leftover pulp from cordial-making in a crumble or fool.

Redcurrants.about: Redcurrants are small, translucent, jewel-like berries that grow in strings and taste bright and sharp. They are a key ingredient in summer pudding and in redcurrant jelly, the traditional British partner for roast lamb. Their short season peaks in July, so freeze some for later.
Redcurrants.choose: Choose glossy, firm berries on fresh green strings, with no shrivelled or squashed fruit.
Redcurrants.store: Keep in the fridge for up to five days, or strip and freeze.
Redcurrants.prep: Strip from the stalks with a fork. Scatter raw over desserts, cook with sugar for jelly and sauces, or mix with raspberries and blackcurrants for summer pudding.
Redcurrants.waste: Cook redcurrants with their stalks for jelly, since the jelly bag strains them out, and freeze any surplus loose to add to crumbles.

Whitecurrants.about: Whitecurrants are a pale, translucent form of the redcurrant, slightly sweeter and less acidic. They are rarely sold in supermarkets, so look for them at farmers' markets and pick-your-own farms in July and August. They look pretty on desserts and are mild enough to eat raw.
Whitecurrants.choose: Choose full strings of plump, translucent berries with no brown, split or shrivelled fruit.
Whitecurrants.store: Keep in the fridge for up to five days, or strip and freeze.
Whitecurrants.prep: Strip from the stalks with a fork and eat raw with yoghurt or cream, scatter over tarts and pavlovas, or cook into a pale jelly.
Whitecurrants.waste: Cook small or bruised whitecurrants down for jelly or a cordial, straining out stalks and seeds, and freeze the rest for summer puddings.

Gooseberries.about: Gooseberries are a very British fruit, with early green ones tart enough for cooking and later dessert varieties, some red or yellow, sweet enough to eat raw. Their sharpness cuts through rich food, which is why gooseberry sauce goes with mackerel. Yorkshire's Egton Bridge has held a gooseberry show for over two centuries.
Gooseberries.choose: Choose firm, unblemished berries; hard green ones are for cooking, while softer, coloured dessert types can be eaten raw.
Gooseberries.store: Keep in the fridge for up to a week, or top and tail and freeze.
Gooseberries.prep: Top and tail with scissors, then stew with sugar for fools, crumbles and pies, or cook down into a sharp sauce for oily fish or pork.
Gooseberries.waste: Stew tough or underripe gooseberries with sugar into a sharp compote for fools and mackerel sauce, and freeze any surplus without topping and tailing.

Blueberries.about: British blueberries are in season from July to September, and home-grown fruit is often larger and juicier than the imports sold the rest of the year. They are sweet and mildly tart, with a pale dusty bloom that shows they have been handled little. They are easy to eat by the handful.
Blueberries.choose: Choose firm, plump, deep blue berries with a silvery bloom, and avoid punnets with soft, wrinkled or mouldy fruit.
Blueberries.store: Keep unwashed in the fridge for up to a week, or freeze on a tray.
Blueberries.prep: Rinse just before eating. Eat raw on porridge and yoghurt, or bake into muffins, pancakes and crumbles, or cook briefly into a compote.
Blueberries.waste: Simmer soft or slightly wrinkled blueberries into a quick compote for pancakes and yoghurt, or freeze them loose to use straight in muffins.

Tayberries & loganberries.about: Tayberries and loganberries are crosses between raspberries and blackberries, with long, dark red berries and a rich, sharp flavour. The loganberry came from California in the 1880s, and the tayberry was bred in Scotland and named after the River Tay. They are soft and travel badly, so look for them at pick-your-own farms and markets.
Tayberries & loganberries.choose: Choose deep red, fully coloured berries that come away easily from the plant, and handle them very gently.
Tayberries & loganberries.store: Eat within a day, keeping them in a single layer in the fridge, or freeze on a tray.
Tayberries & loganberries.prep: Eat raw with cream and sugar, or use as you would raspberries in jams, fools, tarts and summer pudding.
Tayberries & loganberries.waste: Sieve soft or crushed berries into a purée for fools, sauces or drinks, and freeze any you cannot use within a day of picking.

Mulberries.about: Black mulberries look like long blackberries and taste rich, sweet and tart. Many old trees survive in London gardens and parks, some linked to James I's 17th-century attempt to start an English silk industry. The fruit is so soft that it rarely reaches shops, so look out for it from tree owners and at markets in late summer.
Mulberries.choose: Look for fully ripe, almost black, glossy berries that drop at a touch; red ones are still sour.
Mulberries.store: Eat on the day they are picked, keeping them chilled in a single layer if needed, or freeze.
Mulberries.prep: Wear old clothes and handle gently, as the juice stains badly. Eat raw, or use in fools, ice cream, jam, gin and summer pudding.
Mulberries.waste: Mulberries spoil fast, so cook any soft or squashed ones straight away into a compote or jam, or freeze them loose for crumbles.

Figs.about: Figs can ripen outdoors in Britain against warm, sunny walls, and Brown Turkey is the variety most often grown. A ripe fig has soft, purple-brown skin and sweet, jammy red flesh full of tiny seeds. Late summer is when British figs, and the best imports, are at their peak.
Figs.choose: Choose figs that are soft and heavy with a slight droop at the neck, and avoid any that are split, sour-smelling or leaking.
Figs.store: Keep at room temperature if eating that day, otherwise in the fridge for two to three days.
Figs.prep: Eat raw, torn open, with cheese or cured ham, or halve and grill, roast with honey, or bake into tarts.
Figs.waste: Roast or stew split figs with honey, and use a clean fig leaf to infuse custard or cream with a coconut-like flavour, then remove it.

Apricots.about: Apricots are small stone fruit with velvety orange skin and sweet, slightly tart, perfumed flesh. A few English growers, mostly in Kent, now produce apricots in July and August, though most in British shops are imported. Cooking intensifies their flavour, so slightly under-ripe fruit is still useful.
Apricots.choose: Choose fragrant fruit with deep orange colour and a slight give when pressed, avoiding green-tinged, hard or bruised ones.
Apricots.store: Ripen at room temperature, then keep in the fridge for two or three days.
Apricots.prep: Eat ripe ones raw, or halve, stone and roast or poach with honey and vanilla, bake into tarts, or add to lamb tagines.
Apricots.waste: Roast or stew overripe apricots into a compote, and throw the stones away, as the kernels inside are not safe to eat in quantity.

Peaches.about: Peaches have downy skin and juicy, sweet, fragrant flesh, in yellow and white varieties, with flat peaches also common. Most sold in Britain come from southern Europe in summer, though a few are grown under glass here. They are best in high summer, when fruit is picked riper and smells of peach.
Peaches.choose: Choose fragrant peaches that give slightly near the stalk, and avoid any with green patches, bruises or wrinkled skin.
Peaches.store: Ripen at room temperature, then keep in the fridge for two to three days.
Peaches.prep: Eat raw, slice into salads with tomatoes and mozzarella, or halve and grill, roast or poach. Dip briefly in boiling water to slip off the skins.
Peaches.waste: Simmer peach skins with sugar and water for a pink syrup for drinks, and poach or roast overripe peaches rather than throwing them out.

Melons.about: Melons need warmth, so most in British shops are imported, though a few growers raise them under glass in summer. Cantaloupe types such as Charentais have scented orange flesh, while honeydew and Galia are paler and crisper. They are at their sweetest and most fragrant in high summer.
Melons.choose: Choose a melon that feels heavy, smells sweet at the stalk end and gives slightly when pressed there.
Melons.store: Keep whole at room temperature until ripe, then chill and eat within a few days; wrap cut melon well, as it scents the fridge.
Melons.prep: Halve, scoop out the seeds and slice off the skin. Eat chilled with cured ham, in salads with cucumber and mint, or blend into cold soups and sorbets.
Melons.waste: Wash, dry and roast melon seeds with salt like squash seeds, and pickle the firm pale rind with vinegar, sugar and spices.

English grapes.about: Most English grapes go into wine, but a small number of dessert grapes are grown under glass and sometimes outdoors. The Great Vine at Hampton Court, planted in 1768, still bears black Black Hamburg grapes that are sold to visitors in early autumn. English grapes are often smaller and more aromatic than imported ones.
English grapes.choose: Choose bunches with plump grapes firmly attached to green, flexible stems, and a light bloom on the skins.
English grapes.store: Keep unwashed in the fridge for up to a week, rinsing just before eating.
English grapes.prep: Eat with cheese, add to salads, or roast with game birds and sausages. Classic sole Véronique pairs grapes with Dover sole in a cream sauce.
English grapes.waste: Blanch young, unsprayed vine leaves to wrap rice or fish, and roast or freeze grapes that are going soft for snacks and sauces.

Forced rhubarb.about: Forced rhubarb is grown in dark, heated sheds and harvested by candlelight, which gives slender, bright pink stalks with a delicate, sharp flavour. West Yorkshire's Rhubarb Triangle, between Wakefield, Morley and Rothwell, has PDO status for it. It brings colour to the kitchen from January to March, when little else fresh is around.
Forced rhubarb.choose: Choose firm, glossy, bright pink stalks that snap cleanly, avoiding any that are limp or bendy.
Forced rhubarb.store: Wrap in a damp tea towel or bag and keep in the fridge for up to a week.
Forced rhubarb.prep: Trim the ends and any leaf, cut into lengths, then roast or poach gently with sugar so the pieces hold their shape. Use in crumbles, fools, tarts and sharp sauces for mackerel or pork.
Forced rhubarb.caution: Rhubarb leaves are poisonous because of their high oxalic acid content, so cut them off and throw them away; eat only the stalks.
Forced rhubarb.waste: Keep the pink poaching liquid to use as a cordial or in cocktails, and put the leaves on the compost, as they are poisonous.

Outdoor rhubarb.about: Outdoor rhubarb follows the forced crop from spring into summer, with thicker, greener stalks blushed with red and a stronger, sharper flavour. It is a staple of British gardens and allotments. Early stalks in April and May are the most tender; later ones get stringy.
Outdoor rhubarb.choose: Choose firm, crisp stalks that snap cleanly, avoiding limp or very thick ones, which can be tough.
Outdoor rhubarb.store: Wrap in a bag or damp cloth and keep in the fridge for up to a week, or chop and freeze.
Outdoor rhubarb.prep: Trim the ends, peel any stringy outer layer from older stalks, then stew, roast or bake with sugar in crumbles, pies, jams and compotes.
Outdoor rhubarb.caution: Rhubarb leaves are poisonous because of their high oxalic acid content, so cut them off and throw them away; eat only the stalks.
Outdoor rhubarb.waste: Simmer stalk trimmings and peel with sugar for a rhubarb syrup, but put the leaves on the compost, as they are poisonous and must not be eaten.

Seville oranges.about: Seville oranges are bitter oranges from southern Spain, in season from about late December to February.
