Queen scallops.store: Keep covered in the coldest part of the fridge and use within a day.
Queen scallops.prep: Flash-fry in butter with garlic, or grill in the half shell topped with garlic butter and breadcrumbs.
Queen scallops.waste: Queenies usually come with their roe, so cook it along with the meat, and stir any leftovers through pasta or a risotto.

Brown crab.about: The heavy-shelled crab of British waters, prized for its sweet white claw meat and rich, savoury brown body meat. Cromer crab from the Norfolk coast is the best-known name, and Devon and Cornwall land large quantities. The meat is fullest in summer and early autumn.
Brown crab.choose: Choose crabs that feel heavy for their size, and favour cock crabs for more white meat; dressed crab should smell sweet and fresh.
Brown crab.store: Keep cooked crab or picked meat covered in the fridge and eat within two days.
Brown crab.prep: Buy ready cooked or boil live crab in well-salted water for about 15 minutes per kilo, then pick the white and brown meat for sandwiches, salads or pasta.
Brown crab.waste: Roast the cleaned shells for a crab stock or bisque, discarding the grey gills, and mix any leftover brown meat into butter or pasta sauce.

Spider crab.about: A long-legged, spiny crab that arrives off the coasts of Devon and Cornwall in spring. Its sweet, delicate meat is more highly regarded in Spain and France, where most of the British catch is exported. Buying it locally supports south-west fishermen and it is often cheaper than brown crab.
Spider crab.choose: Choose crabs that feel heavy for their size and have all their legs; buy cooked or live from a good fishmonger.
Spider crab.store: Keep cooked crab covered in the fridge and eat within two days.
Spider crab.prep: Boil live crab in salted water for about 15 minutes, then pick the meat from the legs and body; it suits pasta, salads and toast.
Spider crab.waste: Spider crab holds lots of meat in the legs, so pick it carefully, then roast the shells for stock, discarding the gills.

Lobster.about: The European blue-black lobster, caught in pots around the British and Irish coast, turns red when cooked. Its firm, sweet meat is one of the great luxuries of the summer table. Cornwall, Northumberland and the Scottish coast land most of the UK catch, with prices lowest at the height of summer.
Lobster.choose: Choose a lively, heavy lobster with both claws, or ask the fishmonger to cook one for you.
Lobster.store: Keep live lobster in the fridge under a damp cloth and cook the same day; cooked lobster keeps up to two days in the fridge.
Lobster.prep: Boil whole in well-salted water, or split and grill with butter; serve with chips, a green salad or mayonnaise.
Lobster.waste: Roast the shells and head (minus the stomach sac and gills) with tomato and brandy for bisque, or infuse them in oil for a lobster butter.

Langoustines.about: Also called Dublin Bay prawns or Norway lobster, these slim, pale orange shellfish come mostly from Scottish waters. Their sweet, delicate tail meat is closer to lobster than to prawns. Creel-caught langoustines from the west coast of Scotland are the best quality, as they are landed in better condition.
Langoustines.choose: Buy live or very fresh, choosing creel-caught ones with intact shells and no blackening at the head.
Langoustines.store: Cook live langoustines on the day you buy them; cooked ones keep a day or two in the fridge.
Langoustines.prep: Boil or steam for two or three minutes, or split and grill with garlic butter; peel and eat with mayonnaise.
Langoustines.waste: Fry the heads and shells in oil with tomato purée and aromatics, then simmer for a bisque or sauce base.

Clams.about: The UK lands and farms several species, including palourde and Manila clams, mainly from the south coast and Poole Harbour. They are sweet, briny and quick to cook, and best in the colder months. Spaghetti alle vongole is the obvious and best use for them.
Clams.choose: Buy live clams that are tightly closed or close when tapped, with no broken shells and a fresh sea smell.
Clams.store: Keep in a bowl in the fridge covered with a damp cloth and cook within a day or two.
Clams.prep: Soak in salted water to purge any sand, then steam open in a covered pan with wine and garlic.
Clams.caution: Discard any that are open and don't close when tapped before cooking, and any that stay shut after cooking.
Clams.waste: Strain the cooking juices through a fine sieve and use them to finish pasta, soup or chowder; discard any clams that stay closed.

Cockles.about: Small, ribbed bivalves raked from sandbanks around the UK, with famous beds at Penclawdd on the Gower and Stiffkey in Norfolk. They are sweet, salty and chewy, and traditionally eaten from a pot with vinegar and pepper at the seaside. In south Wales they are fried with laverbread and bacon for breakfast.
Cockles.choose: Buy live in the shell from a trusted fishmonger, choosing cockles that are closed or close when tapped.
Cockles.store: Keep in a bowl in the fridge under a damp cloth and cook within a day.
Cockles.prep: Soak in several changes of salted water to remove sand, then steam open; eat with vinegar or add to pasta, rice and chowder.
Cockles.caution: Discard any that are open and don't close when tapped before cooking, and any that stay shut after cooking.
Cockles.waste: Soak cockles to purge sand, then keep the strained cooking liquor for chowder or pasta; leftover meat is good on toast with vinegar.

Razor clams.about: Long, thin clams with a sweet, meaty flavour, dug or hand-dived from sandy beaches around Scotland and Wales. They cook in a minute or two and have a firmer bite than ordinary clams. They look dramatic on the plate and are good value compared with scallops.
Razor clams.choose: Buy live, choosing razors that retract or move when touched and have unbroken shells.
Razor clams.store: Keep in the fridge under a damp cloth and cook the same day or the next.
Razor clams.prep: Rinse, then steam or grill for a minute or two until they open; remove the dark gut, slice the meat and dress with garlic, chilli and herbs.
Razor clams.caution: Discard any that are open and don't close when tapped before cooking, and any that stay shut after cooking.
Razor clams.waste: Save the strained juices from steaming for a dressing or sauce, and chop any leftover meat into a salad or fried rice.

Winkles.about: Small sea snails gathered from rocks around the British coast, traditionally sold cooked in paper bags at seaside stalls and East London shellfish stalls. They have a chewy texture and a sweet, salty, seaweedy taste. They are cheap and plentiful through the colder months.
Winkles.choose: Buy from a trusted fishmonger, choosing live winkles that retract into the shell when touched, or freshly cooked ones.
Winkles.store: Keep live winkles in the fridge under a damp cloth and cook within a day; eat cooked ones within two days.
Winkles.prep: Rinse well and boil in salted water for about five minutes, then winkle out the meat with a pin after removing the little hard cap.
Winkles.caution: Buy only from a reputable supplier and discard any that don't retract when touched before cooking.
Winkles.waste: Pick leftover cooked winkles out with a pin and toss them in garlic butter on toast, or add them to a seafood salad.

Brown shrimp.about: Tiny, sweet grey-brown shrimps caught in shallow waters, most famously in Morecambe Bay and off the Lincolnshire and Norfolk coasts. They are cooked on the boat and are fiddly to peel but full of flavour. Potted in spiced butter, they are a British classic.
Brown shrimp.choose: Buy them cooked, peeled or unpeeled, and look for a sweet smell and a firm, moist texture.
Brown shrimp.store: Keep in the fridge and eat within two days; potted shrimps keep a little longer under their butter seal.
Brown shrimp.prep: Eat on toast, in omelettes or with fish, or pot them in butter spiced with mace and cayenne.
Brown shrimp.waste: Turn leftover peeled shrimp into potted shrimps with spiced butter, and simmer any heads and shells you peel for a quick stock.

Squid.about: Squid come close to the south coast of England in autumn, when Sussex, Devon and Cornwall boats land them, and jig-caught local squid is a world away from frozen imports. The flesh is sweet and tender if cooked very quickly or very slowly. It is good value and suits big flavours.
Squid.choose: Choose squid with glossy, firm bodies, intact skin and a clean sea smell; the bigger the eyes and brighter the skin, the fresher it is.
Squid.store: Keep covered in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within a day or two, or clean and freeze.
Squid.prep: Clean, score and cook fast on a very hot griddle or deep-fry, or braise slowly with tomatoes and wine.
Squid.waste: Use the tentacles and wings as well as the body, fried or chargrilled, and keep the ink sac for black risotto or pasta.

Cuttlefish.about: A relative of squid that comes into the English Channel in spring to spawn, landed mainly in Sussex, Dorset and Devon. The flesh is thicker and sweeter than squid, and the ink is used to colour rice and pasta. Most of the catch is exported to Spain and Italy, so it can be cheap when you find it.
Cuttlefish.choose: Choose shiny, firm cuttlefish with a clean sea smell, and ask the fishmonger to clean it and keep the ink sac if you want it.
Cuttlefish.store: Keep covered in the coldest part of the fridge and cook within a day or two.
Cuttlefish.prep: Grill or fry quickly after scoring, or stew slowly with tomato and wine until tender; use the ink for black risotto.
Cuttlefish.waste: Cuttlefish ink is richer than squid's, so save the sac for risotto nero, and slow-cook the tentacles in a tomato stew.

New-season lamb.about: Lamb born in late winter and spring and eaten from early summer, with pale, tender meat and a mild, sweet flavour. Breed and grazing matter: Welsh lamb, Romney Marsh salt marsh lamb and Herdwick from the Lake District all taste distinctive. It is at its best and best value from late summer into autumn.
New-season lamb.choose: Look for pale pink to light red meat with firm, creamy-white fat, and ask the butcher about the breed and where it was raised.
New-season lamb.store: Store covered in the fridge for up to three days, or freeze.
New-season lamb.prep: Roast legs and shoulders, grill chops and cutlets pink, or slow-cook shoulder until it falls apart.
New-season lamb.waste: Roast the bones from a leg or shoulder for stock, and mince or chop leftover roast lamb for a shepherd's pie or stuffed flatbreads.

Hogget.about: Sheep between one and two years old, with deeper colour, fuller flavour and more fat than young lamb. It fills the gap in late winter and spring before new-season lamb arrives. Hogget from hill breeds is especially good, and many butchers think it has the best balance of tenderness and flavour.
Hogget.choose: Look for darker meat than lamb with good creamy fat cover, and buy from a butcher who hangs it for at least a week.
Hogget.store: Store covered in the fridge for up to three days, or freeze.
Hogget.prep: Slow-roast or braise shoulder and leg, or roast rack and loin pink; it takes strong herbs and spices well.
Hogget.waste: Use the bones for stock and shred leftover slow-cooked shoulder into a pie, a pilaf or a filling for pittas.

Mutton.about: Meat from sheep over two years old, with a deep colour and strong, rich flavour that was standard on British tables until the mid-20th century. It needs long, slow cooking and is good value. Mutton is at its best in autumn and winter, after the sheep have fattened on summer grazing.
Mutton.choose: Choose meat that is deep red with firm, white fat, from a butcher who has hung it for at least two weeks.
Mutton.store: Store covered in the fridge for up to three days, or freeze.
Mutton.prep: Braise, stew or slow-roast for several hours; it is ideal for curries, hotpots and mutton with caper sauce.
Mutton.waste: Simmer the bones with barley and root vegetables for Scotch broth, and skim off the fat once the stock has cooled.

Beef.about: British beef is available all year, with native breeds such as Aberdeen Angus, Hereford and Dexter known for good marbling and flavour. Grass-fed beef from good pasture and properly dry-aged meat taste markedly better than standard supermarket cuts. Slow-cooking cuts come into their own in autumn and winter.
Beef.choose: Choose meat that is deep red with creamy-white fat and good marbling, and ask the butcher how long it has been dry-aged.
Beef.store: Store covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge: steaks and joints for up to three days, mince for one or two.
Beef.prep: Roast rib or sirloin, grill or fry steaks, and braise shin, cheek and brisket slowly in stock or ale.
Beef.waste: Roast bones for a rich stock, save the dripping for roast potatoes, and turn leftover roast beef into hash or sandwiches.

Pork.about: British pork is produced all year, and outdoor-bred or free-range pigs from traditional breeds such as Gloucester Old Spot, Tamworth and Berkshire give richer, more flavourful meat. Good crackling depends on dry, well-scored skin. Autumn apples and pork are a classic British pairing.
Pork.choose: Look for pale pink meat with firm, white fat and dry skin, and choose outdoor-reared pork from a named farm where possible.
Pork.store: Store uncovered or loosely covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge for up to three days.
Pork.prep: Roast belly or shoulder slowly for crackling, grill chops, or braise cheeks and hocks; cook through until the juices run clear.
Pork.waste: Score and roast spare skin for crackling, render any fat for cooking, and use leftover roast pork in fried rice or noodles.

Free-range chicken.about: Free-range chickens have outdoor access and are usually grown more slowly than intensively reared birds, giving firmer meat and more flavour. Breeds such as Label Anglais and Cotswold White are raised for flavour. They are available all year and a whole bird is the most economical way to buy.
Free-range chicken.choose: Choose a plump bird with unbroken, creamy skin and a clean smell, from a butcher or farm that tells you how it was reared.
Free-range chicken.store: Store covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge and use within two days of buying, or by the use-by date.
Free-range chicken.prep: Roast whole, joint and braise, or poach; use the carcass for stock and cook through until the juices run clear.
Free-range chicken.waste: Simmer the carcass with onion and celery for stock, use the giblets for gravy, and render any spare skin and fat for cooking.

Duck.about: Farmed duck is available all year, with Gressingham and Aylesbury the best-known British types. The meat is rich and dark with a thick layer of fat that renders into good roasting fat. Its richness suits sharp fruit such as cherries in summer and oranges in winter.
Duck.choose: Choose a plump bird or breasts with dry, creamy skin and a thick fat layer, and avoid any with a sticky surface.
Duck.store: Store uncovered on the bottom shelf of the fridge so the skin dries, and use within two days.
Duck.prep: Score the breast skin and render it slowly skin-side down before finishing pink; roast whole birds and slow-cook legs.
Duck.waste: Pour off and strain the fat to roast potatoes, and simmer the carcass for stock; leftover legs can be shredded for a pancake filling.

Guinea fowl.about: A bird originally from Africa, farmed in Britain and France, with flesh somewhere between chicken and pheasant: slightly gamey and darker than chicken. It is available all year and makes a good change from chicken for a Sunday roast. The meat is lean, so it benefits from bacon or butter.
Guinea fowl.choose: Choose a plump, firm bird with clean skin, and ask the butcher whether it is free-range.
Guinea fowl.store: Store covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge and use within two days.
Guinea fowl.prep: Roast with butter or bacon over the breast, or joint and braise with wine and mushrooms; cook through until the juices run clear.
Guinea fowl.waste: Pick leftover meat for a pie or salad and simmer the carcass with vegetable trimmings for a light, flavourful stock.

Goose.about: A rich, dark-fleshed bird with plenty of fat, traditionally eaten at Michaelmas (29 September) and at Christmas. Free-range geese are reared on grass through the summer and are ready from autumn. One bird feeds fewer people than its size suggests, but the rendered fat is excellent for roast potatoes.
Goose.choose: Order a free-range goose from a farm or butcher well ahead of Christmas, choosing a plump, dry-skinned bird.
Goose.store: Store loosely covered on the bottom shelf of the fridge and cook within three days of buying.
Goose.prep: Prick the skin and roast on a rack, pouring off the fat as it collects; save it for roasting potatoes.
Goose.waste: Strain and jar the fat, which keeps for months in the fridge, use the giblets in gravy, and simmer the carcass for stock.

Free-range turkey.about: Free-range turkey from slow-growing breeds such as Norfolk Black and Bronze has firmer meat and much more flavour than intensively reared birds. Most are reared for Christmas, with Norfolk the traditional heartland. A properly hung bird cooks faster and stays moister than many cooks expect.
Free-range turkey.choose: Order early from a farm or butcher, ask whether it has been dry-plucked and hung, and buy for the number of people you are feeding.
Free-range turkey.store: Store on the bottom shelf of the fridge, loosely covered, and cook by the use-by date.
Free-range turkey.prep: Roast with butter under the skin and bacon over the breast, and rest it well before carving; cook through until the juices run clear.
Free-range turkey.waste: Boil the carcass for stock, and cool leftover meat within two hours, then use within two days in pies or curries, or freeze.

Grouse.about: Red grouse is a wild bird from the moors of Scotland and northern England, and the season opens on the Glorious Twelfth of August. It has dark, strongly flavoured meat with a heathery taste that comes from its diet. Young birds early in the season are the most tender.
Grouse.choose: Buy from a game dealer or butcher, ask whether it is a young bird, and look for an undamaged breast.
Grouse.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Grouse.prep: Roast young birds hot and fast for about 15 minutes, leaving them pink, and serve on toast with bread sauce; braise older birds.
Grouse.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Grouse.waste: Simmer the carcasses for a dark game stock, and fry the livers to spread on toast; check for lead shot as you eat.

Snipe.about: A small wild wader, shot from August to January, with rich, dark meat and a strong, gamey flavour. Each bird is about one serving for a starter. Like woodcock, it is traditionally cooked with its innards (the trail) left in and served on toast.
Snipe.choose: Snipe is rarely sold, so ask a game dealer; look for plump, well-feathered birds with intact breasts.
Snipe.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Snipe.prep: Roast hot for about ten minutes, then serve on fried bread or toast spread with the cooked innards.
Snipe.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Snipe.waste: Snipe are traditionally roasted whole and served on toast, and the tiny carcasses can go into a game stock with other birds.

Partridge.about: The UK has two kinds: the native grey partridge and the more common red-legged (French) partridge. The meat is pale, tender and mildly gamey, which makes it a good introduction to game. The season opens on 1 September and partridge is at its best in autumn.
Partridge.choose: Buy oven-ready from a game dealer or butcher, choosing plump birds with unbroken skin.
Partridge.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Partridge.prep: Roast hot for about 20 minutes, or pot-roast with cabbage and bacon; one bird serves one.
Partridge.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Partridge.waste: Keep the carcasses after roasting for a game stock or gravy, and use leftover meat in a game pie or salad.

Pheasant.about: The most common game bird in Britain, shot from 1 October to 1 February. Hen birds are smaller and more tender, while cocks are larger. The meat is lean and mildly gamey, and plentiful supply makes it cheap at butchers and game dealers through the winter.
Pheasant.choose: Buy a brace (cock and hen) or oven-ready birds from a game dealer, choosing plump birds with little shot damage.
Pheasant.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Pheasant.prep: Roast with bacon over the breast, or pot-roast and braise to keep the lean meat moist; legs are good slow-cooked.
Pheasant.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Pheasant.waste: Slow-cook the tougher legs into a ragù or rillettes, and simmer the carcass for stock; watch for lead shot in the meat.

Woodcock.about: A small, secretive woodland wader that is among the most prized of British game birds. Its dark meat is rich and deeply flavoured, and it is traditionally roasted with the guts in and served on toast. The shooting season in England runs from October to January.
Woodcock.choose: Woodcock is rarely sold, so ask a game dealer; look for plump, intact birds.
Woodcock.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Woodcock.prep: Roast hot for about 12 to 15 minutes, then serve on fried bread spread with the cooked innards.
Woodcock.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Woodcock.waste: Woodcock is traditionally roasted with its innards, which are spread on toast, and the carcasses add depth to a game stock.

Mallard.about: The largest and most common wild duck in Britain, shot from September to January. It has darker, leaner and gamier meat than farmed duck, with a good depth of flavour. A single mallard serves two, and birds that have fed inland on grain are usually better eating than those from the coast.
Mallard.choose: Buy from a game dealer or butcher, choosing plump birds with intact breasts.
Mallard.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Mallard.prep: Roast whole for about 30 minutes and serve pink, or pan-fry breasts and slow-cook the legs.
Mallard.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Mallard.waste: Render the fat for roasting and simmer the carcass for a game stock; leftover breast meat is good sliced cold in a salad.

Teal.about: The smallest British wild duck, with fine, dark meat that is sweeter and more delicate than mallard. One bird serves one person. The season runs from September to January, and teal is one of the best-flavoured of the wildfowl.
Teal.choose: Teal is rarely sold, so ask a game dealer; look for plump, well-feathered birds.
Teal.store: Store loosely covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Teal.prep: Roast hot for about 15 minutes and serve pink, or pan-fry the breasts quickly.
Teal.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Teal.waste: Teal are small, so roast them whole, then simmer the carcasses with an onion and bay for a small batch of rich stock for gravy, picking out any shot first.

Wild venison.about: Meat from wild red, roe, fallow and muntjac deer, culled to manage numbers across Britain. It is very lean, dark and mildly gamey, and each species has its own open season. It is one of the healthiest and most sustainable meats available.
Wild venison.choose: Ask the butcher which species it is; roe and fallow are milder and more tender, while red deer is more strongly flavoured.
Wild venison.store: Store covered in the fridge for up to three days, or freeze.
Wild venison.prep: Sear loins and haunch steaks quickly and serve pink, or slow-cook shoulder and shin in stews and pies.
Wild venison.caution: Wild venison may contain lead fragments from the bullet, so buy from a trusted dealer and trim around the wound channel.
Wild venison.waste: Ask for the bones and roast them for a dark stock, and mince or dice any trimmings for chilli, ragù or burgers rather than throwing them away.

Hare.about: Brown hare has dark, rich and strongly flavoured meat, quite different from rabbit. Jugged hare, cooked with red wine and thickened with the blood, is the classic British dish. Hare cannot be sold from March to July, so it is an autumn and winter meat.
Hare.choose: Buy from a game dealer, preferably a young hare (leveret), already skinned and jointed.
Hare.store: Store covered in the fridge and cook within two or three days.
Hare.prep: Slow-cook legs in red wine for stews and ragù, and cook the saddle fillets quickly so they stay pink.
Hare.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Hare.waste: After taking the saddle, slow-cook the legs in a ragù for pasta and simmer the carcass with vegetables for stock, checking for and removing any shot.

Wild rabbit.about: Wild rabbit is cheap and available all year in Britain, with no closed season. It is leaner and has more flavour than farmed rabbit, with sweet, pale meat. It is at its best from autumn to spring, and a single rabbit feeds two.
Wild rabbit.choose: Buy from a game dealer or butcher, ideally skinned and jointed, and look for young rabbits with pale, moist meat.
Wild rabbit.store: Store covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Wild rabbit.prep: Braise or slow-cook with mustard, cider or wine to stop the lean meat drying out; the saddle can be roasted quickly.
Wild rabbit.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Wild rabbit.waste: Fry the kidneys and liver in butter on toast, and simmer the carcass and front legs with herbs for a light stock to use in risotto or pie.

Wood pigeon.about: A wild bird shot all year as a crop pest, with dark, lean meat that is milder than most game. The breasts are the main part eaten and are cheap and quick to cook. It is plumpest from late spring to autumn after feeding on crops.
Wood pigeon.choose: Buy whole birds or breasts from a game dealer, choosing plump, deep red breasts with no strong smell.
Wood pigeon.store: Store covered in the fridge and cook within two days.
Wood pigeon.prep: Sear breasts in a hot pan for two minutes a side and serve pink, or slow-cook whole birds in a casserole.
Wood pigeon.caution: Wild-shot game can contain lead shot or fragments, so check as you eat and remove any pellets you find.
Wood pigeon.waste: If you only use the breasts, simmer the legs and carcass with onion and thyme for a rich stock, picking out any shot before straining.

Kentish cobnuts.about: A cultivated hazelnut grown in Kent orchards since Victorian times, most commonly the Kentish Cob variety. They are sold fresh, starting with green husks and white, juicy kernels in August and turning brown and sweeter by autumn. Fresh cobnuts have a milky, slightly sweet crunch quite unlike dried hazelnuts.
Kentish cobnuts.choose: Choose nuts with fresh, unblemished husks and heavy, full shells.
Kentish cobnuts.store: Store in a paper bag in the fridge for up to two weeks.
Kentish cobnuts.prep: Crack and eat raw, or toast them lightly; they suit salads, pesto, crumbles and dishes with game.
Kentish cobnuts.waste: Fresh cobnuts dry out quickly, so shell any spares and freeze them, or toast and chop them into pesto, crumbles or salads before they turn soft.

Hazelnuts.about: Wild hazels grow in hedgerows and woods across Britain, and their nuts ripen in early autumn. The kernels have a sweet, buttery flavour that deepens when toasted. Squirrels often take them before they are ripe, so foragers have to be quick.
Hazelnuts.choose: Choose nuts with full, heavy shells and no holes or cracks, which suggest insects or empty kernels.
Hazelnuts.store: Store in a cool, dry place in their shells for several months, or keep shelled nuts in an airtight jar.
Hazelnuts.prep: Toast to bring out the flavour and loosen the skins, then use in salads, baking, praline or with game and fish.
Hazelnuts.waste: Toast stale hazelnuts to refresh their flavour, then blitz into a nut butter, dukkah or crumble topping; keep spares in the freezer to stop them going rancid.

Wet walnuts.about: Fresh walnuts harvested in early autumn and sold before drying. Their kernels are creamy and mild, with only a hint of the bitterness of dried walnuts. They are a short-season treat, sold for only a few weeks in September and October, and are best peeled before eating.
Wet walnuts.choose: Choose nuts that feel heavy and have clean, unbroken shells with no sign of mould.
Wet walnuts.store: Store in the fridge for up to two weeks, as they spoil faster than dried walnuts.
Wet walnuts.prep: Crack the shells and peel off the bitter skin, then eat with cheese and wine, or use in salads and sauces.
Wet walnuts.waste: Wet walnuts spoil faster than dried ones, so keep them in the fridge, peel the skins if bitter, and freeze any you won't eat within a week.

Sweet chestnuts.about: The nuts of the sweet chestnut tree, which grows widely across southern England, ripen in October. They have a floury texture and sweet, nutty flavour, and roasting them is a winter tradition. They are good in stuffings and soups and with sprouts at Christmas.
Sweet chestnuts.choose: Choose shiny, heavy nuts with no holes or mould, and avoid any that rattle in the shell.
Sweet chestnuts.store: Store in a cool, dry place for a week or in the fridge for up to three weeks.
Sweet chestnuts.prep: Score each nut with a cross and roast or boil, then peel while warm; use in stuffings, soups or with Brussels sprouts.
Sweet chestnuts.caution: If foraging, don't confuse sweet chestnuts (spiky, needle-covered cases holding several flattish nuts) with poisonous horse chestnuts or conkers (thick, sparsely spiked cases holding one round nut), and always score before roasting so they don't burst.
Sweet chestnuts.waste: Freeze leftover cooked chestnuts, then crumble them into stuffing, soups, sprouts or a chestnut and mushroom pie later in the winter.

Firm tofu.about: Firm tofu is soya milk curdled and pressed into blocks, a bit like making fresh cheese. It tastes mild and slightly beany, with a dense, springy texture that soaks up marinades and crisps well. Use it for stir-fries, traybakes, scrambles and anything you want golden and chewy. Some tofu is now made in the UK.
Firm tofu.choose: Look for extra-firm or firm blocks with a short ingredients list of soya beans, water and a coagulant such as nigari or calcium sulphate, ideally organic.
Firm tofu.store: Keep unopened packs in the fridge, then store leftover tofu covered in fresh water in a sealed box, changing the water daily, and use within 3 to 4 days.
Firm tofu.prep: Press it for 20 to 30 minutes under a heavy board, then tear or cube it, toss in cornflour and fry or roast hot until crisp before adding sauce. A marinade of soy, garlic and a little sugar works best after pressing.
Firm tofu.caution: Soya is a common allergen, so check before cooking for guests.
Firm tofu.waste: Crumble offcuts and odd ends into a scramble or stir-fry, or freeze them; frozen and thawed tofu becomes chewier and soaks up marinade well.

Silken tofu.about: Silken tofu is soya milk set in its pack without pressing, so it stays soft, smooth and custard-like. It has a gentle, creamy taste and falls apart if handled roughly. Blend it into creamy sauces, dressings, mousses and cheesecake fillings, or serve it cold in slabs with a punchy dressing.
Silken tofu.choose: Choose soft or firm silken according to use, and look for a short list of soya beans, water and coagulant; long-life cartons keep in the cupboard until opened.
Silken tofu.store: Once opened, keep it covered in the fridge and use within 2 to 3 days.
Silken tofu.prep: Drain it gently and slide it out whole if serving cold, then spoon over soy, chilli oil and spring onions. For sauces, blend it until completely smooth before warming gently.
Silken tofu.caution: Soya is a common allergen, so check before cooking for guests.
Silken tofu.waste: Blend leftover silken tofu into smoothies, creamy pasta sauces or salad dressings, and use it within two to three days of opening.

Smoked tofu.about: Smoked tofu is firm tofu that has been smoked, usually over beech or other hardwood, which gives it a drier, denser texture and a savoury, bacon-like flavour. It can be eaten straight from the pack. Slice it into salads, fry it in cubes as lardons, or add it to stews, pasta and grain bowls.
Smoked tofu.choose: Look for a firm block with a natural smoke process listed rather than smoke flavouring, ideally organic.
Smoked tofu.store: Keep it in the fridge and once opened wrap it tightly and use within 4 to 5 days.
Smoked tofu.prep: It needs no pressing; cut it small and fry in a little oil until crisp at the edges. A splash of soy sauce or maple syrup at the end gives it a sticky glaze.
Smoked tofu.caution: Soya is a common allergen, so check before cooking for guests.
Smoked tofu.waste: Dice the ends and fry them until crisp to scatter over salads, soups or fried rice, where they add a bacon-like smokiness.

Tempeh.about: Tempeh is whole soya beans, cooked and fermented with a culture that binds them into a firm cake. It has a nutty, earthy, slightly mushroomy flavour and a firm, chewy bite, with more fibre and protein than tofu. Tempeh is made in the UK by several small producers, and some use British fava beans or other pulses instead of soya.
Tempeh.choose: Choose a firm block with the beans well knitted together by white mycelium; a few grey or black patches are normal, but avoid anything slimy or sour-smelling.
Tempeh.store: Keep it in the fridge and use within 3 to 4 days of opening, or freeze it for up to 3 months.
Tempeh.prep: Steam or simmer slices for 10 minutes first to soften any bitterness and help it absorb a marinade. Then marinate and fry, grill or roast until browned.
Tempeh.caution: Most tempeh is made from soya, which is a common allergen, so check the pack.
Tempeh.waste: Crumble leftover tempeh and fry it with soy and garlic as a mince for tacos, pasta sauce or rice bowls; it also freezes well.

Seitan.about: Seitan is wheat gluten, the protein left when wheat flour is washed of its starch, cooked into a dense, chewy dough. It tastes of little on its own and takes on whatever it is cooked in, and its meaty, stringy texture suits kebabs, stir-fries, roasts and stews. You can buy it ready-made or make it at home from vital wheat gluten flour.
Seitan.choose: Ready-made seitan should be firm and springy in a seasoned broth; for home-made, buy vital wheat gluten flour, which is pure gluten.
Seitan.store: Keep it covered in its broth in the fridge for up to a week, or freeze it for up to 3 months.
Seitan.prep: Simmer home-made seitan gently in well-seasoned stock rather than boiling it hard, which makes it spongy. Slice thinly and fry hard to get crisp edges.
Seitan.caution: Seitan is pure wheat gluten, so it is unsuitable for anyone with coeliac disease or a wheat allergy.
Seitan.waste: Keep the broth seitan was simmered in and use it as a well-seasoned stock for soups and gravy, and freeze any spare seitan in portions.

Mycoprotein (Quorn).about: Mycoprotein is protein from a naturally occurring fungus, grown by fermentation and sold under the Quorn brand as mince, pieces, fillets and more. It has been made in Teesside and North Yorkshire since the 1980s. It tastes mild, with a fibrous, tender texture, and works in bolognese, curries, pies and stir-fries.
Mycoprotein (Quorn).choose: Check the label: many Quorn products contain egg and are vegetarian, while the vegan range uses potato protein instead, so pick accordingly.
Mycoprotein (Quorn).store: Keep frozen until needed and cook from frozen, or use chilled packs by the date; cooked leftovers keep 2 days in the fridge.
Mycoprotein (Quorn).prep: Brown it well in hot oil before adding liquid, and season boldly, since it takes on flavour easily. Mince needs no extra fat and cooks through in about 10 minutes.
Mycoprotein (Quorn).caution: A small number of people react to mycoprotein, and many Quorn products contain egg, so check the label for allergies.
Mycoprotein (Quorn).waste: Cook frozen Quorn straight from the freezer as needed, and use up leftovers cooked in a pasta bake, chilli or filled jacket potato the next day.

Soya mince (TVP).about: Soya mince, or textured vegetable protein, is defatted soya flour pressed through an extruder and dried into chewy granules. It tastes of very little and is high in protein and cheap, so it is a good stand-by for chilli, bolognese, cottage pie and stuffed vegetables. A small bag rehydrates to a lot of mince.
Soya mince (TVP).choose: Buy plain dried granules or chunks with soya as the only ingredient, ideally from non-GM or organic soya.
Soya mince (TVP).store: Dried TVP keeps for a year or more in an airtight jar; rehydrated or cooked, keep it in the fridge and use within 3 days.
Soya mince (TVP).prep: Soak it for 10 minutes in hot, well-seasoned stock with a dash of soy, squeeze out the excess, then fry it hard in oil until browned before adding sauce.
Soya mince (TVP).caution: Soya is a common allergen, so check before cooking for guests.
Soya mince (TVP).waste: Rehydrate only what you need, and freeze any extra rehydrated mince in portions for a quick bolognese, chilli or cottage pie later.

Plant-based mince.about: Plant-based mince is a ready-made meat alternative usually made from soya, pea or wheat protein, with oil, binders and flavourings. It browns and clumps much like beef mince, so it slots straight into bolognese, lasagne, chilli, burgers and cottage pie. Recipes vary a lot between products in taste, fat and salt.
Plant-based mince.choose: Read the ingredients for the protein source and allergens, and compare salt and saturated fat, since coconut oil is common.
Plant-based mince.store: Keep it chilled or frozen as the pack says; once opened use within 2 days, and cooked mince keeps 2 to 3 days in the fridge.
Plant-based mince.prep: Brown it hard in a hot pan, in batches, and leave it alone until crusty before breaking it up. Add onions, garlic and liquid only once it has coloured.
Plant-based mince.caution: Most plant-based mince contains soya, wheat or pea protein, so check the label for allergens.
Plant-based mince.waste: Freeze leftover raw mince before its use-by date, and turn extra cooked sauce into a lasagne, stuffed peppers or a pie filling.

Plant-based sausages.about: Plant-based sausages are made from soya, pea or wheat protein, or from vegetables, pulses and breadcrumbs, seasoned like pork or Cumberland sausages. Textures range from firm and meaty to soft and herby. Use them in sausage and mash, toad in the hole, casseroles and traybakes, or sliced into pasta.
Plant-based sausages.choose: Check the ingredients for the protein base and allergens, and choose ones with plenty of herbs and pepper in the list.
Plant-based sausages.store: Keep chilled or frozen as the pack says, and once cooked keep them in the fridge for up to 3 days.
Plant-based sausages.prep: Fry or roast them in a little oil over a moderate heat, turning often, since they have less fat than pork sausages and can dry out or split if blasted.
Plant-based sausages.caution: Many plant-based sausages contain wheat gluten or soya, so check the label if you have an allergy or coeliac disease.
Plant-based sausages.waste: Slice leftover cooked sausages into a pasta sauce, bean casserole or breakfast hash, or freeze unopened packs before the use-by date.

Young jackfruit.about: Young jackfruit is the unripe fruit of a large tropical tree, sold tinned in brine or water. It tastes neutral and pulls into strands that look like shredded meat, so it works in pulled 'pork', tacos, curries and burgers. It is low in protein, so serve it with beans or lentils if it's the main event.
Young jackfruit.choose: Buy young or green jackfruit in brine or water, not ripe jackfruit in syrup, which is sweet.
Young jackfruit.store: Once opened, keep it in a covered box in the fridge and use within 3 days; cooked jackfruit keeps 3 days too.
Young jackfruit.prep: Drain and rinse it well, cut out the hard core, squeeze out the water and shred with forks. Fry until it starts to colour, then add a strong sauce and cook until sticky.
Young jackfruit.waste: Shred leftover jackfruit and freeze it in its sauce, or crisp it in a pan for tacos, sandwiches or a topping for loaded fries.

Edamame (frozen).about: Edamame are young green soya beans, picked before they dry and sold frozen, in the pod or podded. They are sweet and nutty with a firm bite, and much higher in protein than garden peas. Eat them in the pod with salt as a snack, or add podded beans to salads, stir-fries, noodles and grain bowls.
Edamame (frozen).choose: Podded beans are handier for cooking, while pods are best for snacking; look for bright green beans with no ice crystals or freezer burn.
Edamame (frozen).store: Keep them frozen and use within a few months; cooked edamame keep 3 days in the fridge.
Edamame (frozen).prep: Boil or steam from frozen for 3 to 5 minutes, then season with flaky salt, chilli or a splash of soy. Don't overcook them or they lose their bite.
Edamame (frozen).caution: Soya is a common allergen, so check before cooking for guests.
Edamame (frozen).waste: The pods are too tough to eat, so pod them before serving; blitz any leftover beans into a green hummus or stir them into fried rice.

British fava beans (dried).about: British fava beans are small, dried broad beans, grown widely in England for centuries and mostly exported until recently. They are earthy and nutty with a creamy texture, and come whole or split. Use split beans for dips, soups and falafel, and whole ones for ful medames and stews.
British fava beans (dried).choose: Split fava beans cook fastest and need no soaking, while whole beans have a skin and need longer; look for UK-grown on the pack.
British fava beans (dried).store: Keep dried beans in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked beans in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen for 3 months.
British fava beans (dried).prep: Simmer split beans for 30 to 40 minutes until soft and creamy. Soak whole beans overnight and cook for about an hour, then dress with plenty of olive oil, lemon, garlic and cumin.
British fava beans (dried).caution: People with G6PD deficiency (favism) should avoid fava beans.
British fava beans (dried).waste: Save the starchy cooking water to thicken soups, and mash leftover cooked beans with garlic, lemon and oil into a dip or ful medames.

Carlin peas.about: Carlin peas are brown dried peas grown in Britain since at least Elizabethan times and eaten in the North East and Lancashire, where they are traditional around Bonfire Night. They taste nutty and earthy, a little like chickpeas, and hold their shape well. Use them in stews, salads, hummus and as a swap for chickpeas.
Carlin peas.choose: Buy them dried and UK-grown, or cooked in tins or jars for speed.
Carlin peas.store: Keep dried peas in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked peas in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen for 3 months.
Carlin peas.prep: Soak overnight, then simmer for about 45 minutes to an hour until tender. Traditionally they are served hot with salt and malt vinegar, and they also brown nicely in a pan with oil and garlic.
Carlin peas.waste: Cook a large batch and freeze extras in their liquid; leftover peas make good fritters, salads or a hummus-style dip.

Yellow split peas.about: Yellow split peas are dried peas with the skins removed and split in half, so they cook down quickly without soaking. They taste mild and sweet and turn soft and creamy. Use them for pease pudding, dal, soups and Greek-style fava dips. Peas for drying are grown in the UK.
Yellow split peas.choose: Buy them dried from a shop with good turnover, since very old split peas take much longer to soften.
Yellow split peas.store: Keep dried split peas in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked ones in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen for 3 months.
Yellow split peas.prep: Rinse well, then simmer for 45 minutes to an hour, skimming off foam, until they collapse. Season at the end and finish with a tarka of fried onion, garlic and spices or a good slug of olive oil.
Yellow split peas.waste: Thin leftover dal or pease pudding with stock to make soup, or bind it with spices and flour into fritters.

Marrowfat peas.about: Marrowfat peas are large, starchy peas left to dry in the field, and almost all are grown in England. They have a sweet, earthy flavour and cook down to the soft texture of mushy peas, the classic partner for chips and pies. They also work in soups and dips.
Marrowfat peas.choose: Dried peas often come with a soaking tablet of bicarbonate of soda; tinned marrowfat or processed peas are ready to heat.
Marrowfat peas.store: Keep dried peas in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked ones in the fridge for 3 days or frozen for 3 months.
Marrowfat peas.prep: Soak overnight with a teaspoon of bicarbonate of soda, rinse well, then simmer for 30 to 40 minutes until soft and mash with salt. Finish with mint or a dash of malt vinegar.
Marrowfat peas.waste: Turn leftover mushy peas into fritters with a little flour, or loosen them with stock and mint for a quick pea soup.

Chickpeas.about: Chickpeas are round, nutty pulses with a firm, creamy texture. They are good for hummus, curries, stews, salads and roasting until crunchy, and the liquid from the tin, aquafaba, whips like egg white for meringues and mousses. Dried chickpeas cooked at home taste noticeably better than tinned.
Chickpeas.choose: Jarred Spanish chickpeas are softer and plumper than most tins; for dried, buy from a shop with good turnover, since old ones never soften fully.
Chickpeas.store: Keep dried chickpeas in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked ones in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen in their liquid for 3 months.
Chickpeas.prep: Soak dried chickpeas overnight, then simmer for 1 to 2 hours until very tender, adding salt near the end. For crisp chickpeas, dry them thoroughly and roast at 200C for 25 to 30 minutes.
Chickpeas.waste: Save the liquid from tins or home-cooked chickpeas as aquafaba to whip into meringues or use as an egg replacer, and roast leftover chickpeas as a snack.

Red lentils.about: Red lentils are split lentils without their skins, so they cook fast and collapse into a thick, creamy purée. They are mild and slightly sweet. Use them for dal, soups, thickening stews and sauces, and in vegan bolognese or shepherd's pie.
Red lentils.choose: Buy dried red lentils from a shop with good turnover, and pick out any small stones as you rinse.
Red lentils.store: Keep dried lentils in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked ones in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen for 3 months.
Red lentils.prep: Rinse well and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes with no soaking, stirring now and then so they don't catch. Finish with fried garlic, spices and a squeeze of lemon.
Red lentils.waste: Leftover dal keeps for three days in the fridge; thin it with stock for soup or use it as a base for a lentil shepherd's pie.

Green & Puy-style lentils.about: Green and Puy-style lentils are small whole lentils that keep their shape when cooked, with a peppery, earthy flavour and a slight bite. Puy lentils are a protected type from France, and similar small green and black lentils are now grown in small amounts in England. Use them in warm salads, braises, soups and as a base for roast vegetables.
Green & Puy-style lentils.choose: Choose small, slate-green or speckled lentils for salads that hold their shape; larger green lentils soften more and suit soups.
Green & Puy-style lentils.store: Keep dried lentils in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked ones in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen for 3 months.
Green & Puy-style lentils.prep: Simmer without soaking for 20 to 30 minutes with a bay leaf and garlic until just tender, then drain and dress while warm with olive oil, vinegar and mustard.
Green & Puy-style lentils.waste: Dress leftover cooked lentils with vinaigrette for a lunch salad, or stir them into soups, stews or a veggie ragù.

Butter beans.about: Butter beans are large, flat, creamy white beans, also called lima beans, with a soft, buttery texture and mild flavour. They are good braised with tomatoes, mashed as an alternative to potato, blended into dips, or roasted until crisp at the edges. Large jarred butter beans are especially creamy.
Butter beans.choose: Jarred beans are plumper and creamier than most tinned ones; for dried, look for large, unbroken, pale beans.
Butter beans.store: Keep dried beans in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked ones in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen in their liquid for 3 months.
Butter beans.prep: Soak dried beans overnight, then simmer gently for 1 to 1.5 hours, as hard boiling breaks their skins. Bake them in a rich tomato sauce or warm them through with olive oil, garlic and herbs.
Butter beans.caution: Dried butter beans must be soaked and cooked thoroughly, never eaten raw or undercooked.
Butter beans.waste: Keep the liquid from tins or home-cooked beans as aquafaba or to make stews creamier, and mash leftover beans on toast with garlic and lemon.

Black beans.about: Black beans are small, shiny dried beans with a dense, creamy inside and a deep, slightly sweet, earthy flavour. They are central to Latin American cooking: use them in chilli, burritos, tacos, soups and bean burgers. Their cooking liquid turns dark and is good for thickening stews.
Black beans.choose: Choose tins with just beans, water and salt, or dried beans that are glossy and unbroken.
Black beans.store: Keep dried beans in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked ones in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen in their liquid for 3 months.
Black beans.prep: Soak overnight, boil hard for 10 minutes, then simmer for about an hour until soft, with onion, garlic and a bay leaf. Season well and finish with lime and fresh coriander.
Black beans.caution: Dried black beans contain a natural toxin, so after soaking they must be boiled hard for at least 10 minutes; slow cookers alone do not get hot enough.
Black beans.waste: Use the dark cooking liquid in soups and stews for body, and fry leftover beans with spices for burritos, quesadillas or a quick dip.

Haricot beans.about: Haricot beans, also called navy beans, are small, oval white beans with a mild flavour and a soft, creamy texture. They are the bean in baked beans, and are good in cassoulet-style stews, soups and white bean mash. Some are now grown in England.
Haricot beans.choose: Choose tins of plain haricot beans in water, or dried beans that are smooth, white and unbroken.
Haricot beans.store: Keep dried beans in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked ones in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen in their liquid for 3 months.
Haricot beans.prep: Soak overnight, boil hard for 10 minutes, then simmer for 45 minutes to an hour until creamy. For home-made baked beans, cook them slowly in tomato sauce with a little treacle and mustard.
Haricot beans.caution: Dried haricot beans contain a natural toxin, so after soaking they must be boiled hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering.
Haricot beans.waste: Freeze cooked beans in their liquid, and turn leftover homemade baked beans into a soup or a jacket potato topping.

British quinoa.about: Quinoa is the seed of a plant related to spinach and beetroot, and it has been grown in England since the 2010s. It cooks to small, fluffy grains with a nutty, grassy taste and a slight pop, and it contains all the essential amino acids. Use it in salads, grain bowls, stuffings and porridge.
British quinoa.choose: Look for UK-grown quinoa, and check whether it has been pre-washed to remove the bitter coating.
British quinoa.store: Keep dried quinoa in an airtight jar for up to a year, and cooked quinoa in the fridge for 3 to 4 days or frozen for 2 months.
British quinoa.prep: Rinse well in a sieve, then simmer in 2 parts water to 1 part quinoa for 12 to 15 minutes, cover and leave to steam for 5 minutes before fluffing. Toasting it dry in the pan first deepens the flavour.
British quinoa.waste: Cook extra and freeze it flat in bags, then add leftovers to salads, soups or veggie burgers, or fry it until crisp as a topping.

Hemp seeds.about: Hulled hemp seeds, sometimes sold as hemp hearts, are the soft inner part of the hemp seed, and hemp is grown for food in England. They taste mild and nutty, a bit like pine nuts, and are rich in protein and omega-3 fats. Sprinkle them over porridge, salads and soups, or blend them into milk, pesto and dressings.
Hemp seeds.choose: Buy hulled seeds for eating raw, and look for UK-grown where you can find them.
Hemp seeds.store: Keep them in an airtight jar in the fridge, where they last a few months; their oils go rancid more quickly at room temperature.
Hemp seeds.prep: Use them raw or only lightly toasted, since high heat spoils the delicate oils. Stir them through dishes at the end of cooking.
Hemp seeds.waste: Store opened hemp seeds in the fridge to stop them turning rancid, and use up the end of a bag in pesto, porridge or smoothies.

White asparagus.about: White asparagus is grown under mounded soil so it never sees light and stays pale. The spears from Germany and the Dutch province of Limburg are thicker than British green asparagus, with a milder, sweeter and faintly bitter taste. The short spring season, April to June, is celebrated in both countries.
White asparagus.choose: Pick straight, firm spears with tightly closed tips and moist, freshly cut ends that squeak when rubbed together.
White asparagus.store: Wrap in a damp tea towel and keep in the fridge for two to three days.
White asparagus.prep: Peel thickly from just below the tip down, as the skin is tough, then simmer in salted water with a pinch of sugar and a knob of butter until tender. Serve with hollandaise or melted butter, new potatoes and ham.
White asparagus.waste: White asparagus needs peeling, so simmer the peelings and woody ends in water for a delicate stock to use in soup or risotto.

Wild asparagus.about: Wild asparagus is a thin, wiry species picked in spring from scrubland in Spain and Italy, and increasingly cultivated there too. It tastes grassier and more bitter than garden asparagus, with a slight bite. A small bunch goes a long way in egg dishes, rice and pasta.
Wild asparagus.choose: Look for bright green, pencil-thin stems that snap cleanly and tips that are tight and not wet or slimy.
Wild asparagus.store: Keep wrapped in damp kitchen paper in the fridge and use within two to three days.
Wild asparagus.prep: Snap off the woody lower stems and use the tender tops. Fry briefly in olive oil and stir into scrambled eggs or a frittata, or add to risotto at the end of cooking.
Wild asparagus.waste: Snap off the tough ends and add them to a vegetable stock, and fold any leftover cooked spears into an omelette or risotto.

Agretti.about: Agretti, also called monk's beard or barba di frate, is a succulent green from Italy, sold in bunches of fine, chive-like stems in early spring. It has a crisp texture and a clean, slightly salty, mineral taste, a little like samphire but milder. The season is short, so it is worth buying when you see it.
Agretti.choose: Choose bright green, springy bunches with no yellowing, and check that the roots and stems are not slimy.
Agretti.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within two to three days.
Agretti.prep: Trim the roots, wash well as it can be gritty, then blanch for one to two minutes. Dress with olive oil and lemon, toss through spaghetti with garlic and chilli, or serve with fish and eggs.
Agretti.waste: Agretti wilts within a few days, so trim the roots and use it quickly; leftover cooked agretti is good in an omelette or pasta.

Spring artichokes.about: Spring artichokes from Italy and France are the smaller, often purple-tinged types, such as Italy's violetto and the round Roman varieties. Picked young, they have little or no hairy choke and tender inner leaves, so far more of the head is edible than on a large globe artichoke. The flavour is nutty and slightly sweet.
Spring artichokes.choose: Pick heavy heads with tightly closed leaves that squeak when squeezed and a fresh-looking stem.
Spring artichokes.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge for up to five days, though they are best cooked soon.
Spring artichokes.prep: Rub cut surfaces with lemon as you go, pull off the tough outer leaves, trim the tops and peel the stem. Braise with garlic, mint and olive oil Roman style, fry, or shave the youngest ones raw into salads.
Spring artichokes.waste: Peel the stems and cook them with the hearts, as they taste much the same; rub cut surfaces with lemon to stop them browning.

Cime di rapa.about: Cime di rapa, or turnip tops, is a leafy green with small broccoli-like buds, closely tied to Puglia in southern Italy. It is in season through autumn, winter and early spring. The flavour is bitter, peppery and mustardy, stronger than purple sprouting broccoli, and it stands up well to garlic, chilli and anchovy.
Cime di rapa.choose: Choose bunches with fresh, dark leaves and tight green buds, avoiding any with yellow flowers opening.
Cime di rapa.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge and use within three days.
Cime di rapa.prep: Strip off thick stems and chop. Boil with orecchiette for the last few minutes, then toss with garlic, chilli and anchovies softened in olive oil, or braise and serve with sausages.
Cime di rapa.waste: Peel the thicker stalks and cook them with the leaves and buds, and stir leftovers into pasta with garlic, chilli and anchovy.

Puntarelle.about: Puntarelle is the cluster of hollow shoots at the heart of Catalogna chicory, a winter speciality of Rome and Lazio. The shoots are crisp, juicy and pleasantly bitter, a little like a cross between chicory and fennel. Sliced thin and dressed with anchovy, it makes one of the best winter salads.
Puntarelle.choose: Look for firm, pale green heads with plenty of fat, closely packed shoots and fresh, unwilted outer leaves.
Puntarelle.store: Keep wrapped in the fridge for up to five days.
Puntarelle.prep: Separate the shoots, slice them lengthways into thin strips and soak in iced water for 30 minutes or so until they curl. Drain well and dress with crushed garlic, anchovy, vinegar and olive oil; the outer leaves can be cooked like chard.
Puntarelle.waste: After using the shoots for salad, cook the outer leaves like chicory, sautéed with garlic and chilli or added to a bean soup.

Radicchio di Treviso.about: Radicchio di Treviso is a red chicory from the Veneto. The early type has long, tight heads; the late type, tardivo, is forced in running water in winter to produce curling, claw-like spears with white ribs. Both are crisp and bitter, milder and more elegant than round radicchio, and hold up well to grilling.
Radicchio di Treviso.choose: Pick firm heads with glossy, deep red leaves, bright white ribs and a fresh, unbrowned base.
Radicchio di Treviso.store: Keep wrapped in the fridge for up to a week.
Radicchio di Treviso.prep: Halve or quarter lengthways, brush with olive oil and grill or roast until wilted and charred at the edges. Use raw in salads with orange, or stir into risotto.
Radicchio di Treviso.waste: Use tougher outer leaves in risotto or grilled with oil and balsamic, and wilt any limp leftovers into pasta with sausage or blue cheese.

Padrón peppers.about: Padrón peppers are small green peppers from Galicia in north-west Spain, named after the town of Padrón. They are thin-skinned with a fresh, grassy flavour, and most are mild, though the odd one is hot. Spanish greenhouses supply them most of the year, with the best in summer.
Padrón peppers.choose: Choose glossy, firm, bright green peppers about the size of a thumb, with no soft or wrinkled patches.
Padrón peppers.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge for up to a week.
Padrón peppers.prep: Leave the stalks on, fry in a little hot olive oil until blistered and collapsing, then scatter with flaky sea salt and eat with your fingers. Good with drinks, alongside grilled fish or in an omelette.
Padrón peppers.waste: Chop leftover blistered peppers into a tortilla, omelette or pasta, or blend them into a romesco-style sauce.

Avocados.about: Avocados from southern Spain, mainly around Málaga and Granada, reach UK shops from autumn to spring, chiefly the dark, knobbly-skinned Hass. They have a buttery texture and a rich, nutty flavour, and travel a much shorter distance than fruit from South America. Most are sold firm and ripen at home.
Avocados.choose: Choose fruit that feels heavy and yields to gentle pressure near the stalk end, avoiding any with dents or sunken patches.
Avocados.store: Ripen at room temperature, then keep ripe ones in the fridge for two to three days.
Avocados.prep: Halve, twist apart and remove the stone, then scoop out the flesh. Mash on toast with lemon and chilli, slice into salads or make guacamole; squeeze over citrus to slow browning.
Avocados.waste: Mash overripe avocados with lemon or lime juice and freeze for guacamole or smoothies; discard the stone and skin rather than eating them.

Black truffle.about: The black winter truffle is an underground fungus found among oak and hazel roots in France, Italy and Spain, and is often called the Périgord truffle. Its season runs from about December to March. It has a deep, earthy aroma and a firm, marbled flesh, and a small amount flavours a whole dish.
Black truffle.choose: Buy from a trusted supplier and look for firm truffles with a strong, clean aroma and dark flesh marbled with fine white veins.
Black truffle.store: Wrap in kitchen paper in an airtight container in the fridge, change the paper daily and use within a week.
Black truffle.prep: Brush clean and shave or grate over hot food; gentle warmth brings out the aroma. Store eggs alongside it in a sealed box for a day to scent them, or fold into butter for pasta, risotto and mashed potato.
Black truffle.waste: Store truffle in a closed jar with whole eggs to perfume them, and grate any small trimmings into butter to freeze for later.

White truffle.about: The white truffle is a pale, knobbly underground fungus found in Italy, most famously around Alba in Piedmont, as well as in parts of central Italy. The season runs from about October to December. Its aroma is strong, garlicky and musky, and it is always used raw, shaved thinly over simple, rich food.
White truffle.choose: Buy from a trusted supplier and look for firm, pale truffles with no soft or damp spots and a powerful aroma.
White truffle.store: Wrap in kitchen paper in an airtight container in the fridge, change the paper daily and use within three or four days.
White truffle.prep: Brush clean and never cook it; shave thinly over buttered tagliatelle, risotto, fried or scrambled eggs, or a plain fonduta just before serving.
White truffle.waste: Keep white truffle in a closed container with eggs or rice to absorb the aroma, then use the eggs and rice for risotto or scrambled eggs.

Satsumas.about: Satsumas are a seedless mandarin type with loose, baggy skin that peels very easily. Spain, chiefly the Valencia region, supplies the UK from about October to December, earlier than clementines. They are sweet, juicy and mild, with soft segments, though they are more delicate than clementines and don't keep as long.
Satsumas.choose: Choose fruit that feels heavy with bright skin that is loose but not puffy, dry or soft.
Satsumas.store: Keep in the fridge and eat within a week, as they soon go dry and puffy.
Satsumas.prep: Peel and eat as they are, or add segments to winter salads and fruit salads. The juice and zest work in dressings and glazes.
Satsumas.waste: Dry the peel in a low oven or on a radiator and add it to stews, stocks and spice rubs for a gentle citrus flavour.

Navel oranges.about: Navel oranges are seedless eating oranges with a small second fruit at the blossom end that looks like a navel. Spain supplies them from about November to spring, with varieties such as Navelina early in the season and Lane Late towards the end. They are sweet, juicy and easy to peel and segment.
Navel oranges.choose: Choose heavy, firm oranges with fine-textured, unblemished skin and no soft spots.
Navel oranges.store: Keep in a cool place for a week or in the fridge for up to three weeks.
Navel oranges.prep: Peel and eat, or slice into salads with fennel, beetroot or red onion. Drink the juice straight away, as navel orange juice turns bitter if it stands for a while.
Navel oranges.waste: Zest the fruit before eating or juicing and freeze the zest, and candy strips of peel in sugar syrup to keep for baking.

Lemons.about: Lemons in UK shops come largely from Spain, mainly Murcia, and from Italy, especially Sicily, and are available all year. Spanish and Italian lemons tend to be juicy with fragrant, oily zest. Their sharp acidity brightens almost anything, from fish and vegetables to dressings and baking.
Lemons.choose: Choose heavy, firm lemons with fine, glossy skin, and buy unwaxed if you plan to use the zest.
Lemons.store: Keep in a bag in the fridge for three to four weeks.
Lemons.prep: Roll firmly on the worktop before squeezing to get more juice, and zest before you cut. Use the juice in dressings and marinades, and finish fish, greens and roast chicken with zest and juice.
Lemons.waste: Zest lemons before squeezing and freeze the zest, and put squeezed halves in a jar of vinegar to make a citrus cleaner.

Amalfi lemons.about: Amalfi lemons are the large, pointed Sfusato Amalfitano variety from the terraced slopes of the Amalfi coast in Campania, protected by an IGP. They have thick, very fragrant peel, a sweet pith that can be eaten, and juice that is less sharp than ordinary lemons. They are the classic fruit for limoncello.
Amalfi lemons.choose: Choose heavy, unwaxed fruit with bright yellow, fragrant skin; a few attached leaves are a sign of freshness.
Amalfi lemons.store: Keep in the fridge for up to three weeks.
Amalfi lemons.prep: Slice very thinly, peel and pith included, and dress with olive oil, salt and herbs as a salad. Use the zest and juice in pasta with butter and parmesan, risotto, curd, cakes and limoncello.
Amalfi lemons.waste: The thick, mild pith is pleasant to eat, so slice Amalfi lemons thinly into salads, and candy or preserve the peel in salt.

Bergamot.about: Bergamot is a knobbly, yellow-green citrus grown almost entirely along the coast of Reggio Calabria in southern Italy, in season over the winter months. Its peel oil gives Earl Grey tea its flavour. The juice is sour and slightly bitter, so the fruit is used for its zest and juice rather than eaten.
Bergamot.choose: Choose firm, heavy fruit with fragrant, unwaxed skin and no soft or brown patches.
Bergamot.store: Keep in the fridge for up to two weeks, or freeze the zest and juice separately.
Bergamot.prep: Use the zest in curds, cakes, ice cream and marmalade, and the juice like lemon in dressings or with raw and grilled fish and scallops. Wash your hands after zesting.
Bergamot.caution: Bergamot peel oil is phototoxic, so skin splashed with it and then exposed to sunlight can redden and blister.
Bergamot.waste: Bergamot juice is sour and bitter, so use it like lemon in dressings, and candy the fragrant peel or infuse it into sugar.

Persimmons (kaki).about: Persimmons, or kaki, are orange, tomato-shaped fruit, and the UK's supply comes largely from the Ribera del Xúquer area of Valencia in Spain, from about October to January. The main Spanish variety, Rojo Brillante, is treated after picking so it can be eaten while firm and crisp. The flesh is sweet and honeyed, like apricot and mango.
Persimmons (kaki).choose: Choose glossy, deep orange fruit with a fresh green calyx and no bruises or cracks.
Persimmons (kaki).store: Keep firm fruit at room temperature for a few days or in the fridge for up to two weeks; very soft ones should be eaten within a day or two.
Persimmons (kaki).prep: Eat firm ones sliced like an apple, skin on, in salads with chicory, rocket and nuts. Scoop out very ripe, jelly-soft fruit with a spoon or use the pulp in puddings and baking.
Persimmons (kaki).caution: Astringent varieties must be fully ripe and jelly-soft before eating, as underripe ones are very high in tannin.
Persimmons (kaki).waste: Very ripe, jelly-like persimmons make a good purée for cakes, smoothies or ice cream, and the skin of firm varieties is fine to eat.

Kiwi fruit.about: Italy is one of the world's largest kiwi growers, mainly in Lazio and Piedmont, and France grows them in the south-west, with fruit from both in UK shops from about November to spring. The usual green Hayward variety is tangy and sweet with soft flesh and tiny edible seeds. They are rich in vitamin C.
Kiwi fruit.choose: Choose plump fruit without wrinkles or bruises that gives slightly when pressed if you want to eat it now.
Kiwi fruit.store: Ripen at room temperature, faster in a bag with an apple, then keep in the fridge for up to a week.
Kiwi fruit.prep: Halve and scoop out with a teaspoon, or peel and slice into fruit salads and onto pavlova. Kiwi contains an enzyme that stops gelatine setting and softens dairy, so add it at the last moment.
Kiwi fruit.caution: Kiwi fruit is a recognised allergen and can cause mouth itching or more serious reactions in sensitive people.
Kiwi fruit.waste: Kiwi skin is edible if you scrub off the fuzz, and overripe fruit can be blended into smoothies or a dressing for fruit salad.

Spanish strawberries.about: Most strawberries in UK shops between about January and May come from Huelva in Andalusia, which grows the bulk of Europe's early crop. They are bred to be firm and travel well, so they tend to be less fragrant and sweet than British berries in midsummer. They are useful for cooking, purées and baking before the home crop arrives.
Spanish strawberries.choose: Look for berries that are red right up to the stalk, glossy and fragrant, and check the bottom of the punnet for mould or juice.
Spanish strawberries.store: Keep unwashed in the fridge for two to three days and bring to room temperature before eating.
Spanish strawberries.prep: Wash just before hulling. Macerate with a little sugar and lemon juice or balsamic vinegar to boost flavour, or roast or bake with forced rhubarb.
Spanish strawberries.waste: Infuse hulls and green tops in water or vinegar for a light flavour, and cook soft, overripe berries into a quick compote.

Peaches & nectarines.about: Peaches and nectarines from Spain, Italy and France fill UK shops from about June to September. Nectarines are smooth-skinned peaches; both come with yellow or white flesh, the white being sweeter and less acidic. A ripe continental peach is juicy and fragrant, ideal eaten over the sink or grilled.
Peaches & nectarines.choose: Choose fruit that smells sweet and gives slightly near the stalk; green patches near the stalk mean it was picked too early.
Peaches & nectarines.store: Ripen at room temperature, then keep in the fridge for two to three days and bring back to room temperature to eat.
Peaches & nectarines.prep: Eat as they are, slice into salads with tomatoes and mozzarella, or halve, stone and grill or roast with honey. Blanch briefly in boiling water if you want to slip off the skins.
Peaches & nectarines.waste: Cook bruised or overripe fruit into compote or jam, and simmer the peelings in sugar syrup to flavour drinks; don't eat the stone kernels.

Flat peaches.about: Flat peaches, also called doughnut or Saturn peaches, are squashed-looking white-fleshed peaches grown widely in Spain, especially Murcia, Aragon and Catalonia, from about June to September. They are sweet, low in acidity and lightly almond-scented, with thin, less fuzzy skin and a small stone that comes away easily.
Flat peaches.choose: Choose fragrant fruit with a creamy rather than green background colour that gives a little at the centre.
Flat peaches.store: Keep at room temperature for a day or two to ripen, then in the fridge for up to three days.
Flat peaches.prep: Eat as they are, skin and all, or halve and stone for fruit salads and tarts. They are also good grilled briefly and served with yoghurt and honey.
Flat peaches.waste: Slice overripe flat peaches into a crumble, compote or smoothie, or freeze them in slices for later baking; discard the stones.

Continental apricots.about: Apricots from Spain, chiefly Murcia, start in May, followed by French fruit from Roussillon and the Rhône valley, including the well-regarded Bergeron variety, through to August. When ripe they are soft, sweet and tart with a honeyed scent. Imported fruit is often picked firm, and cooking brings out its flavour.
Continental apricots.choose: Choose deep orange fruit with a velvety skin and a sweet smell that gives slightly when pressed, avoiding pale or green-tinged ones.
Continental apricots.store: Ripen at room temperature, then keep in the fridge for two to three days.
Continental apricots.prep: Halve and stone, then roast or poach with honey and vanilla, bake into tarts and clafoutis, or add to lamb tagines. Ripe ones are good eaten as they are.
Continental apricots.caution: Don't eat the kernels from inside the stones in quantity, as they contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide when digested.
Continental apricots.waste: Halve and freeze overripe apricots, or cook them into jam or compote; don't eat the kernels inside the stones, as they can be toxic.

Charentais melons.about: Charentais melons are small, round cantaloupe-type melons from western and southern France, with smooth grey-green skin marked by darker stripes. The deep orange flesh is very sweet, juicy and strongly perfumed, with more scent than most other melons in UK shops. The season runs from about June to September.
Charentais melons.choose: Choose a melon that feels heavy, smells sweet and musky at the stalk end, and gives slightly there when pressed; a few fine cracks round the stalk are a good sign.
Charentais melons.store: Keep at room temperature until ripe, then wrap cut melon tightly and keep in the fridge for two to three days.
Charentais melons.prep: Halve, scoop out the seeds and serve in wedges, chilled but not ice-cold. Classic with cured ham and black pepper, or with mint and a splash of port.
Charentais melons.waste: Blend the seeds and the pulp around them with water, strain and sweeten for a refreshing drink, and freeze leftover chunks for smoothies.

Watermelon.about: Watermelons from Spain, mainly Almería and Murcia, are in UK shops from about May to September, and many are now seedless. The flesh is crisp, very juicy and refreshingly sweet. It is good in salads as well as on its own, especially paired with salty cheese, chilli and herbs.
Watermelon.choose: Choose a heavy melon with a creamy yellow patch where it rested on the ground and a hollow sound when tapped.
Watermelon.store: Keep whole in a cool place for up to two weeks; wrap cut pieces and keep in the fridge for three to four days.
Watermelon.prep: Cut into wedges or cubes and serve chilled. Toss with feta, mint and olive oil, blend into drinks, or grill thick slices briefly to concentrate the sweetness.
Watermelon.waste: Pickle the white rind with vinegar, sugar and spices, and blend or freeze leftover flesh for juice, granita or ice lollies.

Italian grapes.about: Italian grapes come mainly from Puglia and Sicily, from about July into December. Varieties include the large, golden Italia with a light muscat flavour and seeds, the red Red Globe and a growing range of seedless types. Late-season Sicilian grapes from Canicattì and Mazzarrone are grown under cover to keep them going into winter.
Italian grapes.choose: Choose plump grapes firmly attached to green, flexible stems, with a light natural bloom and no shrivelled or split fruit.
Italian grapes.store: Keep unwashed in the fridge for up to a week and rinse just before eating.
Italian grapes.prep: Serve with cheese, roast with rosemary and olive oil to go with game or sausages, or press into focaccia. Halve and seed larger grapes for salads.
Italian grapes.waste: Freeze spare grapes as a snack or to chill drinks, and roast softening grapes with herbs to serve with cheese or sausages.

Mirabelle plums.about: Mirabelles are small, round golden plums, often freckled red, from Lorraine in north-eastern France, where Mirabelle de Lorraine is protected by an IGP. The season is short, from about mid-August to mid-September. They are sweet and honeyed with firm flesh and a stone that pulls away easily, making them good for eating and baking.
Mirabelle plums.choose: Choose firm, golden-yellow fruit with a light bloom and a fresh scent, avoiding green or split plums.
Mirabelle plums.store: Keep in the fridge for up to five days, or halve, stone and freeze for later.
Mirabelle plums.prep: Eat as they are, or halve and stone for tarts, clafoutis, jam and compote. They hold their shape well when baked and go well with roast pork and duck.
Mirabelle plums.waste: Halve, stone and freeze surplus mirabelles for crumbles, or cook overripe fruit into jam or compote; discard the stones rather than eating the kernels.

Plant-based burgers.about: Plant-based burgers are vegan patties made to resemble beef burgers. They are typically made from pea or soya protein, sometimes with wheat gluten, held together with binders and given fat from coconut or rapeseed oil, often coloured with beetroot juice. They are convenient and high in protein, and they cook quickly.
Plant-based burgers.choose: Read the label for protein, salt and saturated fat levels, and check the allergens if you need to.
Plant-based burgers.store: Keep in the fridge and use by the date on the pack, or freeze for up to three months.
Plant-based burgers.prep: Fry or grill on a medium-high heat until browned and piping hot all the way through, following pack timings. Serve in toasted buns with sliced tomato, lettuce, red onion and chips.
Plant-based burgers.caution: Many contain soya, gluten, mustard or celery, so check the allergen list on the pack.
Plant-based burgers.waste: Crumble a leftover cooked burger into a pasta sauce or chilli, and freeze unopened packs before the use-by date.

Plant-based chicken pieces.about: Plant-based chicken pieces are vegan strips or chunks made to replace chicken in everyday cooking. They are typically made from soya protein or wheat gluten, sometimes pea protein, processed to give a fibrous, chicken-like texture. They have a mild taste that takes on marinades and sauces well, and many cook straight from frozen.
Plant-based chicken pieces.choose: Check the label for protein content and salt, and whether the pieces are plain or already seasoned.
Plant-based chicken pieces.store: Keep chilled pieces in the fridge until the use-by date and frozen ones in the freezer as the pack directs.
Plant-based chicken pieces.prep: Stir-fry, roast or add to curries and wraps towards the end of cooking, as they can dry out. Marinating for 15 minutes first adds plenty of flavour.
