Plant-based chicken pieces.caution: Many contain soya or gluten, so check the allergen list on the pack.
Plant-based chicken pieces.waste: Toss leftover cooked pieces into a stir-fry, wrap or pasta salad the next day, or freeze unopened packs before the use-by date.

Plant-based bacon.about: Plant-based bacon is a vegan alternative sold as thin rashers. It is usually made from wheat gluten or soya protein, sometimes with pea protein, coloured and flavoured with smoke, salt and a little sugar. It crisps up well in a pan and adds a smoky, savoury note to sandwiches and vegetable dishes.
Plant-based bacon.choose: Check the ingredients and salt level, and look for rashers that are evenly sliced so they cook evenly.
Plant-based bacon.store: Keep in the fridge, use within a few days of opening and by the use-by date, or freeze.
Plant-based bacon.prep: Fry in a little oil over a medium heat for a couple of minutes each side, as it burns more easily than pork bacon, and let it crisp as it cools. Use in sandwiches, with leeks and sprouts, or crumbled over soups and pasta.
Plant-based bacon.waste: Freeze rashers in small portions so you only cook what you need, and chop leftovers into carbonara, soups or a hash.

Plant-based meatballs.about: Plant-based meatballs are vegan balls made to resemble beef or pork meatballs. They are typically made from soya or pea protein, sometimes with wheat gluten, seasoned with onion, garlic and herbs. They hold their shape well in sauce and are a quick, high-protein option for pasta dishes, subs and traybakes.
Plant-based meatballs.choose: Check the label for protein and salt levels, and look for ones that are seasoned to suit how you plan to cook them.
Plant-based meatballs.store: Keep in the fridge and use by the date on the pack, or freeze for up to three months.
Plant-based meatballs.prep: Brown in a pan or oven, then simmer gently in tomato sauce for the last few minutes so they heat through without falling apart. Serve with spaghetti, in rolls, or with mash and gravy.
Plant-based meatballs.caution: Many contain soya, gluten or celery, so check the allergen list on the pack.
Plant-based meatballs.waste: Freeze leftover meatballs in their sauce for a later meal, or slice them into a sub roll with cheese and tomato sauce.

Halloumi.about: Halloumi is a firm, brined cheese from Cyprus, traditionally made from sheep's and goat's milk, often with cow's milk added. It has a springy, squeaky texture and a salty, milky taste, and its high melting point means it browns in the pan without collapsing. Some halloumi is made with animal rennet, so check the label if you are vegetarian.
Halloumi.choose: Look for a firm, tightly sealed block and check the label for vegetarian rennet if that matters to you.
Halloumi.store: Keep unopened in the fridge until the date on the pack; once opened, keep in its brine or wrapped and use within three days, or freeze.
Halloumi.prep: Pat dry, slice about 1cm thick and fry or grill in a dry or lightly oiled pan until golden on both sides. Eat hot, as it turns rubbery when cool, with salad, watermelon or grilled vegetables.
Halloumi.caution: Halloumi is high in salt, so keep portions modest if you are watching your salt intake.
Halloumi.waste: Keep leftover halloumi submerged in its brine or lightly salted water in the fridge, and grate any dry ends over salads or into fritters.

Paneer.about: Paneer is a fresh, unaged cheese from South Asia, made by curdling hot milk with lemon juice or vinegar, then pressing the curds into a block. It is made without rennet, so it is suitable for vegetarians. It has a mild, milky flavour and a firm texture that does not melt when heated, making it ideal for curries and grilling.
Paneer.choose: Choose a firm, evenly white block with a fresh, milky smell, and check the use-by date.
Paneer.store: Keep in the fridge; once opened, store submerged in water in a covered container, changing it daily, and use within three days, or freeze.
Paneer.prep: Cut into cubes and fry until golden, then soak in hot water for a few minutes to soften before adding to curries. It is also good marinated in spiced yoghurt and grilled on skewers.
Paneer.waste: If you make your own paneer, save the whey for bread dough, dal or soups, and freeze leftover paneer cubes for a later curry.

Free-range eggs.about: Free-range eggs come from hens with continuous daytime access to an outdoor range. They are available all year and are an inexpensive, complete source of protein for vegetarians. Freshness matters more than shell colour: very fresh eggs have firm whites that hold their shape when poached or fried.
Free-range eggs.choose: Check the best-before date, look for uncracked shells and a British Lion mark, and buy the freshest you can find for poaching.
Free-range eggs.store: Keep in their box in the fridge, away from strong smells, and use by the best-before date.
Free-range eggs.prep: Use the freshest eggs for poaching and frying and slightly older ones for boiling, as they peel more easily. Scramble with chives, bake with spinach and leeks, or make a frittata with whatever vegetables are in season.
Free-range eggs.caution: Eggs are a common allergen, and only eggs with the British Lion mark are advised as safe to eat runny for pregnant women and other vulnerable groups.
Free-range eggs.waste: Freeze spare egg whites for meringues or omelettes, and use leftover yolks within two days for mayonnaise, custard or carbonara.
